docs.title: Gerda
docs.text:
Gerda — open-source bot framework by Flamerix AI.

In memory of Gerda, a much-loved dog. This project carries her name.

Why it exists. Heavy modpacks like Monifactory are wonderful, and they ask for more evenings than most of us have. Gerda is for playing them anyway: send a bot, or an AI agent driving it, to do the routine grind and the boring crafting, and keep the fun parts for yourself.

Gerda is two things. The harness is a framework for running bot code inside Minecraft on the jsMacros mod: a TCP bridge, an MCP server for LLM operators, screenshots and GUI input, and a worker that drives any Module tick by tick. It works without our bot (harness/bot_template.js). Gerda Bot is our reference bot on top of it: an autonomous ore-mining bot and multi-bot fleet for GregTech CEu (Monifactory, Forge 1.20.1). It plays as a real, non-op player with no extra server-side mods; its only privilege is the pack's FTB Essentials teleport.

New here? Setup from zero takes you from an empty machine to a driven bot. The repo README has the feature tour, and examples/ has templates from basic to advanced.

docs.title: How Gerda works
docs.text: This page is a map. It names each part, says what it is for, and points at the code that holds it. The code is the reference: when this page and the code disagree, the code wins.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Gerda has two parts. The harness (harness/) is a set of plain-JS jsMacros services that run inside the Minecraft client: a TCP bridge, a supervisor that answers commands, and a worker that loads a bot and drives it one game tick at a time. Gerda Bot (src/) is our reference bot: a TypeScript kernel that tsup (tsup.config.ts) compiles to one file, dist/__gerda_bot.bundle.js. That bundle assigns globalThis.Module, and the worker eval-loads it. The script engine is GraalJS (ECMAScript 2022). The harness accepts any object with the Module contract, not only ours: harness/bot_template.js is a plain-JS skeleton.

docs.title: The command path
docs.text:
A command from the host travels through five boxes. Each box has one job.

 host                 │  inside the Minecraft client (jsMacros services)
                      │
 bridge_ctl.py ──┐    │
                 ├─TCP:55544─► bridge.js ──GlobalVars──► main.js
 MCP server "mc" ┘    │                                    │ 1. HANDLERS  (built-in, screen.js)
                      │                                    │ 2. EXT       (ext.js plugins)
                      │                                    │ 3. passthrough
                      │                                    ▼  GlobalVars
                      │                                 worker.js ──tick──► Module
                      │                                                  (dist/__gerda_bot.bundle.js)
Box Role Code Host clients Send newline-framed JSON requests and read the correlated reply scripts/ops/bridge_ctl.py, mcp/server.py, mcp/bridge_client.py bridge Zero-logic TCP gateway: queues each request into GlobalVars, relays the reply harness/bridge.js main Always-on supervisor: routes a command to a built-in handler, then to an ext plugin, then to the worker harness/main.js#dispatch, routing rule harness/safe-io.js#route (TS twin src/shared/harness/dispatch.ts#routeDispatch) ext Hot-reloadable mod-API plugins (EMI, prospector, FTB Quests, camera…) harness/ext.js, registry harness/main.js#register eyes and hands Screenshots and synthetic GUI input, merged into main's handlers harness/screen.js worker Loads the bundle, calls Module.command and Module.tick, writes a heartbeat harness/worker.js#loadBundle, harness/worker.js#processCommand Module The bot. Ours is built in src/bot/entry/worker-bundle.ts#makeModule src/bot/entry/worker-bundle.ts

The services share no module system. They talk only through GlobalVars keys, and every key and envelope shape is defined once in harness/ipc.js (TS twin src/core/ipc/ipc.ts). The wire protocol, the key tables and the tick pacing are in IPC.md.

docs.text:
src/ is layered core < shared < bot. An import may only point down a tier, so a fork can take core/ alone, or core/ + shared/, without our bot.

Tier What lives there Key entry points src/core/ The only boundary over jsMacros and Java, the IPC envelope, dependency-free primitives. Pack-agnostic. src/core/runtime/Runtime.ts#Runtime, real impl src/core/runtime/jsmacros/index.ts#createJsMacrosRuntime, mock twin src/core/runtime/mock.ts#createMockRuntime, SRG tokens src/core/runtime/jsmacros/srg.ts src/shared/ The reusable engine: kernel, navigator, pure domain logic, config schema, reflexes, the harness twins src/shared/kernel/, src/shared/nav/, src/shared/domain/, src/shared/reflexes/, src/shared/config/schema.ts src/bot/ Gerda Bot: capabilities, missions, plans, the orchestrator, the pack profile, entry wiring. The only tier that knows GregTech. src/bot/capabilities/, src/bot/missions/, src/bot/plans/, src/bot/orchestrator/, src/bot/profile/, src/bot/entry/worker-bundle.ts

The defensive checker refuses an outward import: rule no-outward-tier-import in scripts/defensive-rules.ts#scanTierImports, run by scripts/check-defensive.ts as part of bun run check. The same checker holds the other reliability rules; they are listed in EXTENDING.md § Reliability rules.

Domain code in src/shared/domain/ takes plain data and never sees the runtime. Everything that touches the game goes through the Runtime facade, so the whole kernel runs against the mock in test-ts/.

docs.title: One tick of the bot
docs.text:
jsMacros fires a tick listener about 20 times a second. One pass, in order:

  1. Worker tick body — harness/worker.js, the body passed to IPC.paceTick (harness/ipc.js#paceTick, which arms the next listener only after this one returns). It bumps the heartbeat, mirrors the render-thread-only reads that main.js publishes (world signature, nearby entities), runs at most one queued command through Module.command, then calls Module.tick, then drains the bundle's events into the shared event ring. A throw out of Module.tick halts the worker and publishes the fault.
  2. Kernel tick — Module.tick is src/shared/kernel/capability.ts#Kernel.tick:
  3. heartbeat guards run first and never preempt (Kernel.runAlwaysGuards; for example src/bot/capabilities/telemetry.ts);
  4. with no mission running, only the survival reflexes run (Kernel.runSurvivalGuards), plus the handler of a safety landing phase, and the tick ends;
  5. otherwise the always-on guards run in registration order, then the active mission's guards (Kernel.runGuards). The first guard that returns true ends the pass;
  6. if no guard ended it, the handler for the current phase runs (Kernel.runHandler): the active mission's handler first, else an always-on one;
  7. when the mission reports done, the mission sequencer picks what runs next;
  8. last, the progress watchdog checks that the running phase advanced (Kernel.checkProgress, policies in src/shared/kernel/progress.ts).
  9. Reflexes — the safety guards in src/shared/reflexes/index.ts#reflexes. The array order is the evaluation order, and makeModule registers them right after the lifecycle capability, so they run ahead of every other always-on guard and every mission guard. They divert only to the universal landings. Which reflexes run while idle: SAFETY.md.
  10. Phases and transitions — the bot's phase vocabulary and edges are data in src/bot/profile/states.ts (STATE, TRANSITIONS, GLOBAL_EDGES, UNIVERSAL_TARGETS, assembled as GERDA_PHASES). The kernel builds one src/shared/kernel/fsm.ts#Fsm from those edges plus each capability's and the active mission's edges (Kernel.buildFsm). An illegal transition throws IllegalTransitionError; a universal target is reachable from any phase.
  11. Capabilities, missions, plans — a capability (src/shared/kernel/capability.ts#Capability) bundles a guard, per-phase handlers, commands and edges. A mission (src/shared/kernel/mission.ts#Mission, often built with missionFromCaps) is one goal machine; the kernel runs one at a time. A plan (src/bot/orchestrator/plan.ts#Plan) is data: an ordered list of mission steps. The orchestrator (src/bot/orchestrator/index.ts#makeOrchestrator) is an always-on capability that also installs the kernel's sequencer (src/shared/kernel/sequencer.ts#MissionSequencer).
  12. Navigator — the only thing that moves the bot. Phase handlers call src/shared/nav/executor.ts#greedyStep once per tick through the @/shared/nav barrel (src/shared/nav/index.ts). Route planning and its caches are in src/shared/nav/route.ts, the pure planners in src/shared/domain/planner.ts and src/shared/domain/dstar.ts; the engine choice is the slice in src/shared/nav/engine.ts.

A capability or mission throw is caught once, at the kernel's dispatch boundary (Kernel.dispatch). A throw from an always-on owner is a core bug and halts the worker; a throw from a mission owner drops only that mission to ERROR.

docs.title: Per-bot client instance setup & tuning
docs.text: How to add one bot as its own launcher instance (Prism/MultiMC/FreesmLauncher — adjust to your launcher) and tune it to use the least host resources while still able to mine and fight. Companion to the server runbook. Each bot is an ordinary MC client running the bundle inside jsMacros.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Each bot is a full modded Minecraft client, so the host ceiling for N of them is memory, not CPU. On hosts with strict memory overcommit (vm.overcommit_memory=2), a client crashes with mmap failed once the system-wide Committed_AS reaches CommitLimit, even with RAM free. Modpack instances often ship a large heap; at, say, -Xmx16G -Xms8G per instance, four bots would reserve 64 GB. Nobody watches a bot, so desktop render settings (render distance 12, 90 fps, fancy graphics, AO, mipmaps, shadows) are waste × N. A low heap and a render floor make 4+ bots on one host viable.

docs.title: 1. Create a bot instance
docs.text:
Each bot = its own instance so its options.txt, account, mods, and bridge port are independent (two bridges cannot share one port).

  1. Clone the play instance. In your launcher, right-click Monifactory → Copy instance, name it Monifactory_bot_<N> (the _bot_ part matters, see the naming contract below). Cloning guarantees the exact mod-set + version the server handshake requires — see the monilabs parity note in SERVER_SETUP § 3a.
  2. Offline account. Accounts → add an offline account with a unique username (bot_<N>). Then pin each instance to its account, so no instance rides the launcher's globally active one. Close the launcher GUI first (it rewrites instance.cfg on close):
./gerda bind-accounts   # = python3 scripts/ops/bind_instance_accounts.py; idempotent

It binds Monifactory_bot_1…_4 to bot_1…bot_4, your play instance to humanAccountName and the shader camera to cameraAccountName; both names come from local.config.json (local.config.json.example), and it stops with an error if one is missing. 3. Connect. Launch it, Multiplayer → Direct Connection → 127.0.0.1:25565 (or launch with the launcher's -s 127.0.0.1:25565 flag, which joins on its own). Leave the bot non-op: it plays like a real player (FLEET_PLAYBOOK § 1). 4. Deploy the bundle. just sync (or ./gerda sync = scripts/ops/sync.py) ships the bundle to every instance and gives each its own bridge port. Verify: ./gerda ctl --bot Monifactory_bot_<N> ping → pong.

docs.title: Naming, accounts and ports — the contract
docs.text:
The host tools find instances by name. This is the one place the rules are written down:

  • Your play instance keeps its plain name: Monifactory by default. If yours is named differently, set humanInstance in local.config.json. Host tools that read your screen or quest book use it.
  • Every bot instance name contains _bot_. The fleet hub dispatches queued tasks and pushes its routine updates only to *_bot_* instances, and refuses to pin a task to any other name, so it never drives your own client unasked. Monifactory_bot_<N> is the convention. An instance that runs a bot under another name (one game instance, with the bot account in it) joins the fleet when you list it in local.config.json "fleetInstances": ["Monifactory"].
  • Instance name vs player name. --bot, the MCP target= and mc-bots.json use the instance name (Monifactory_bot_2). In game and in the server console, the bot is its account name (bot_2).
  • One offline account per instance, each with a unique username. The server runs online-mode=false, so no paid account is needed. Two instances cannot be online under the same username at once.
  • Bridge ports. just sync gives every instance that has a jsMacros Macros folder its own bridge port, writes it to that instance's bridge_port.txt, and records it in the gitignored mc-bots.json (two bridges cannot share a port). A newly seen instance gets the lowest free port from 55544 up, and keeps it on every later sync. On a first sync the instances are taken in name order, so Monifactory gets 55544 and Monifactory_bot_1 gets 55545; an instance you add later takes the next free port. mc-bots.json holds the actual ports, and --bot <instance> looks them up there.
  • The tuner's default set. ./gerda tune with no arguments tunes every instance whose name contains _bot_ that mc-bots.json or your launcher's instances folder knows. It never tunes your play instance (humanInstance), and it stops with an error when it finds no bot instance. Name an instance to tune only that one.

docs.title: 2. Tune it for minimum resource use
docs.text:
# stop the bot first — a RUNNING MC rewrites options.txt on quit and would clobber the edit.
./gerda tune Monifactory_bot_<N>     # = python3 scripts/ops/tune_bot_instance.py
# no args = every *_bot_* instance in mc-bots.json or the instances folder (never humanInstance)

./gerda tune (scripts/ops/tune_bot_instance.py) is idempotent and edits two files. It deliberately leaves enableVsync:false (off-screen screenshots need it) and guiScale:4 (the eyes/hands click math is screenshot-pixel ÷ 4) untouched.

options.txt (render floor):

key value why renderDistance / simulationDistance 5 ~64-block sensory horizon — enough for mining, local nav, melee hunt; the bot's World.getBlock/entity sensing only sees loaded chunks, and the server simulates in MP anyway maxFps 30 the bot tick runs on the worker thread, not the render thread, so it isn't fps-bound; screenshots/clicks are event-driven. 30 just trims GPU/CPU graphicsMode 0 (fast) no fancy/fabulous ao entityShadows renderClouds bobView off cosmetic-only biomeBlendRadius / mipmapLevels 0 drop colour-blend + texture-mip work entityDistanceScaling 0.75 render-cull only — entities still exist in the client world for hunt sensing particles 2 (minimal) soundCategory_master 0.0 mute → no sound-engine cost

instance.cfg (heap): OverrideMemory=true, MinMemAlloc=2048, MaxMemAlloc=4096. 4 GB max fits a render-5 bot; low Xms stops the JVM from committing a large heap up front at launch. Bump to 5–6 GB only if a specific bot OOMs under heavy chunk loading (GTCEu registry spikes).

GOTCHA — instance.cfg is launcher-owned, not game-owned. Prism, MultiMC and FreesmLauncher cache each instance's settings in memory and rewrite instance.cfg from that cache (on instance launch / settings-dialog save / launcher exit), so editing the file while the launcher is running is clobbered — the bot launches with the old heap and you get duplicate keys. Set the heap one of two ways: (a) in the GUI — Edit Instance → Settings → Memory → override → Max 4096 / Min 2048 (authoritative, writes the file cleanly); or (b) run the tuner with the launcher fully CLOSED, then reopen. The tuner detects your own running Prism, MultiMC or FreesmLauncher by process name and then skips the heap edit; another user's launcher and a defunct (zombie) launcher process do not count. A launcher that runs under another process name is not detected, so close it yourself first. options.txt has no such problem — it's read by MC itself at game launch, so the tuner's render edits stick as long as that bot is stopped when you run it.

docs.title: Combat-ready vs minimal — the dial
docs.text:
The bot stays fully combat-capable under all of the above: bot logic reads server-driven world and entity state on the worker thread, independent of render quality. Two knobs trade capability for resources:

  • renderDistance is the bot's sensory horizon. 5 is the floor for mine/hunt; raise to 6–8 if a mission needs more lookahead, drop to 4 for absolute minimum.
  • maxFps can go to 10–15 for the leanest GPU footprint; keep ≥30 if you screenshot-drive the GUI rapidly (each screenshot forces a render, but a higher cap keeps the off-screen frame fresher between shots).

docs.title: 3. Apply to the already-running bots
docs.text: Editing a running instance's options.txt is futile — MC overwrites it from memory on quit. So tune each running bot while stopped: in the launcher, stop bot → run the tuner for it → relaunch. The heap change (instance.cfg) only takes effect on the next launch regardless.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• A no-GL client: vanilla MC needs a GL context. For an off-screen client see RIG.md § Run.
  • Removing mods: client-only mods (jsMacros, EMI, JourneyMap) power the bot's own features, and removing server-matched mods breaks the handshake. Render settings give the savings without that risk.

docs.title: How Gerda was built
docs.text:
Gerda — open-source bot framework by Flamerix AI.

Gerda is a framework for writing and running bot code inside Minecraft on the jsMacros mod. Gerda Bot is the reference implementation on it: an autonomous ore-mining bot, and a small co-op fleet, for the GregTech CEu modpack Monifactory on Minecraft 1.20.1. It prospects veins, walks to them with its own navigator, digs them out, hauls the ore home, smelts, crafts a spare pickaxe so a worn one can be swapped out and goes back out. The bots join a co-op server as ordinary non-op players. Nobody hands them items in fleet play: they earn what they use.

This page is about what we found while building it and how we solved it.

docs.title: No LLM in the runtime loop
docs.text:
The bot is ordinary deterministic code: a TypeScript kernel, compiled to one bundle that the jsMacros mod runs inside the game client, 20 ticks a second. At runtime nothing calls a model. The API cost is zero, there is no latency spike while a prompt runs, and the same world state gives the same decision.

An LLM can drive it. The repo ships a standard MCP server (mcp/server.py) that exposes live bots as tools: mc_get_state, mc_send, and fleet calls such as "a free bot, go get iron". Nothing in the bot depends on it: with no MCP client attached, the bots keep playing.

How this differs from well-known neighbours:

  • Voyager is a research system in which an LLM writes and refines its own skill code as it plays. The LLM is the learner.
  • Mindcraft puts an LLM in charge of an in-game agent you can talk to. Great for conversation and open-ended play; every decision is a model call.
  • Baritone is an excellent pathfinding utility. We learned a lot from its movement model before writing our own navigator.

Gerda Bot takes a third route: plain code that plays on its own, with an LLM as an optional driver rather than a dependency.

docs.title: By the numbers
docs.text:
• src/ is 156 TypeScript files, ~24k lines, plus ~16k lines of tests.
  • The tests: vitest suites for the kernel and Python suites for the host tooling. TESTING.md has the current count.

docs.title: What we found, and what we built
One seam to the game, with a mock that cannot drift
docs.text: Only one layer, the runtime facade, may touch jsMacros. It is a TypeScript interface with two implementations: the real one and an in-memory mock. Because both implement the same interface, the mock cannot drift: add a method to the real runtime and the mock stops compiling. This is why the whole test suite runs in seconds without Minecraft.

docs.title: Our own navigator
docs.text:
A mining bot keeps changing the world under its own path, and Baritone's standalone build exposes no Java API to scripts — only chat commands and position polling. So Gerda Bot has its own navigator: A* over a cached world view (D* Lite optional, off by default), and a greedy executor with sub-machines for ladders, pillaring, bridging and sprint-jump parkour. Hazard vetoes keep it out of lava, water traps and pits it cannot climb back from.

We measured before switching. navbench races navigators on identical legs in the live game: ours arrives on every leg, like Baritone, and is within 13 % on speed; the slower legs come from deliberate safety margins. Ideas from Baritone (movement physics, goal types, block traits) live on as data. See navbench.md.

docs.title: Forge member names are SRG — resolved offline
docs.text:
On Forge 1.20.1, class names are readable but class members keep obfuscated SRG names (m_7583_, f_91073_). GraalJS resolves members by their real name, so mc.level by its readable name is simply undefined. Our answers:

  • Ask the jsMacros facade, not raw fields. Player.getPlayer() != null tells you the client is in a world; a raw-field probe cannot.
  • Look names up offline. srg.py resolves Mojang ↔ SRG names from the mapping files the launcher already has on disk, with Parchment parameter names when available. No trial calls in game.
  • Call by Mojang name. srg('Player','getFoodData') resolves the SRG name at runtime, and a boot self-check verifies every hardcoded token against the current pack's map.
  • Read the source. decompile.sh decompiles the game or any mod jar to Mojang-named source.

docs.title: Guarding the render thread
docs.text: A command that blocks the render thread for more than 500 ms makes jsMacros kill the handler, and a long block can drop the world. Three guards keep the game responsive: the jeval escape hatch rejects blocking code before it runs, the bridge restarts a stalled supervisor, and a lint rule stops committed harness code from blocking the render thread.

docs.title: GraalJS threading and number coercion
docs.text: GraalJS binds each JS context to one thread, so timed sequences are driven from the host over separate bridge calls, never by closures handed between threads. A JS number passed to a Java float parameter must be exactly representable as a float, so the facade wraps such values in Math.fround().

docs.title: Verify effects, not attempts
docs.text: The water-bucket clutch places water under the bot mid-fall to survive long drops. It aims and retries every tick while the drop point is in reach, leads the aim by the horizontal drift, and counts the clutch as done only when the bucket is actually empty. The same rule runs through the kernel: eating is confirmed by the food level, a teleport by the position change, a deposit by re-reading the bag.

docs.title: A camera that moves every frame
docs.text: Setting the player's rotation once per tick looks jerky on film. The camera client instead hooks Forge's per-frame ViewportEvent.ComputeCameraAngles, registered from GraalJS through the explicit-class addListener overload, so camera moves are smooth at any frame rate.

docs.title: Off-screen capture
docs.text: The rig runs each client inside its own headless sway compositor with a 60 Hz output and records it with wf-recorder. Nothing appears on the monitor.

docs.title: The film rig is a feature
docs.text:
We shot our teaser with the same harness (RIG.md). Bot and camera clients boot inside headless compositors. Scenes are staged from data and re-armed between laps, and a scripted camera flies smooth moves; inside a lap, the bot's moves are its own. The clutch shot starts with a scripted step off the ledge, and catching that fall is the bot's reflex. Takes are accepted by measurement: a motion probe rejects frozen or dead footage. The cut is assembled from a JSON cut list with burned-in captions.

On set, too, the bots play as real players: they are non-op on our co-op server, and the camera client is the only op. The scenes around them are staged, from the sets to the items the camera drops to the bot; RIG.md lists what is staged and how.

docs.title: How we work
docs.text:
We build it with Claude Code; the process is built to catch mistakes before they land:

  • The git hooks are the gate. In-game tests cannot run in CI, and pure checks belong at commit time. pre-commit runs tsc, biome, a defensive-code checker and vitest; pre-push repeats them, adds the Python suites, and builds and validates the bundle.
  • Fail loudly. The defensive-code checker rejects try/catch, as casts, empty catch blocks and dropped Results outside a few boundary files. Fallible game reads return a typed Result, never a made-up default. A core bug halts the worker; a mission bug drops only that mission to ERROR. A silent 0 would hide the bug from whoever reads the log next.
  • One trunk, one worktree per task. Everything lands on one trunk by fast-forward. Each task, human or agent, runs in its own git worktree, so parallel work doesn't collide.
  • Independent review. For changes that matter, a separate review agent, which never saw the author's reasoning, tries to break the diff before it lands.
  • Every test has a known-bad twin. Each positive test is paired with an input that must fail. A gate never seen rejecting anything proves nothing.
  • Write it down. CLAUDE.md and docs/EXTENDING.md are the onboarding that every contributor, human or agent, reads first. When an approach is dropped, the reason and the evidence are written down at once, so nobody retries it blind.

docs.title: What carries over to your project
docs.text:
1. Measure the runtime before designing for it.
  2. One typed seam to the outside world, with a mock that cannot drift.
  3. Make the gate local and hard to skip.
  4. Fail loudly. Silent fallbacks turn into false beliefs later.
  5. Verify effects, not attempts.
  6. Write down why an approach was dropped, when you drop it.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Gerda Bot and the bundled mod plugins are tuned to Monifactory and GregTech CEu: ore registry, prospector and quests. The portability guide maps what carries over to other packs and versions. Movement physics and real block breaking have no mock, so in-game behaviour is checked by a manual live gate (just gate-live). Run the bots only on servers that allow automation.

docs.title: Build your own bot on the harness
docs.text:
Who this is for: you want the game-access plumbing — a TCP bridge, a worker that drives a Module tick-by-tick, eyes/hands, MCP for LLM operators — but not our mining bot — say a farmer, a courier or an arena fighter. This page shows the floor (how little you must adopt) and the ceiling (how much of our stack you can pull in).

Gerda is two things and this doc is about keeping them separate: Gerda the harness (the plain-JS jsMacros services) runs any bot; Gerda Bot (src/) is our reference implementation that happens to ship in the same repo. Everything below replaces the second while reusing the first.

docs.title: The three layers — floor to ceiling
docs.text:
The harness is not a monolith — it's three separate jsMacros services (bridge, main, worker) you register one by one, talking only through GlobalVars keys (all defined in one file, ipc.js). So the floor is even lower than "write a Module": register bridge + main only and you have remote game control with no bot at all — status, scan, inventory, eval/jeval, screenshots and GUI clicks, every ext.js plugin, the whole MCP surface. Worker-passthrough commands just fail loudly; nothing else cares. A bot only enters the picture when you register the worker: your code must then produce a Module object (init / tick / command / stop, optional describe / onChat) that worker.js eval-loads under the fixed bundle name __gerda_bot.bundle.js. Everything above that is a choice.

Layer You register / adopt… Build step Proof / template 0 — primitives only, no bot bridge + main (+ ext.js) none remote-drive the game from the host: examples/basic/drive_bot.sh, the MCP server 1 — plain-JS bot + worker; nothing but the Module contract none harness/bot_template.js 2 — TS bot on the Runtime facade src/core/runtime/ (the only mandatory TS layer) tsup examples/advanced/standalone-bot.ts — a complete bot in a small fraction of the full bundle 3 — the whole kernel, à la carte FSM/capabilities, nav, reflexes, missions — pick what you want tsup EXTENDING.md, examples/

(For completeness: bridge alone is a deliberate zero-logic pipe — newline-framed JSON ↔ GlobalVars — so "keep the bridge + MCP, replace main with your own GlobalVars consumer" is a documented seam, but exotic; the practical floor is bridge + main.)

Take an arena fighter as the example. The navigator (src/shared/nav/) is probably useful to any bot that has to walk somewhere without falling in a hole — take it. The reflexes (water clutch, swim-out, stuck watchdog) are useful if your bot roams dangerous terrain — maybe take them. The missions (drill, chop, search…) are ours — they encode our mining-economy goals, so unless you're mining you'll write your own on the same seam. Layer 3 is a menu, not a package.

docs.title: Recipe — a plain-JS bot, no build step
docs.text:
The fastest path. No TypeScript, no tsup, no node_modules even.

  1. Copy harness/bot_template.js to yourbot.js and fill in init / tick / command / stop. All bot memory lives in the state object the harness threads through those calls — never in module-level variables (the worker can reload the bundle at any tick). The template is Apache-2.0, so your bot can use any license. Keep the last line, globalThis.Module = MyModule;: worker.js reads the global, and in a strict-mode file a var Module never leaves the worker's eval (the worker then loads no module and says so in get_state.worker.fatal).
  2. Deploy it as the worker bundle and reload the worker: ./gerda sync -s yourbot.js -n __gerda_bot.bundle.js, then ./gerda ctl send reload_worker. worker.js loads the bundle by that fixed name, so your file takes the place of Gerda Bot; ./gerda sync without -s puts Gerda Bot back. With more than one instance, add --only <instance>: without it the file goes into every instance, and another running bot loads it at its next worker reload.
  3. Drive it: ./gerda ctl send my_start, ./gerda ctl send my_target '{"x":100,"y":64,"z":200}'. Every command the container does not own reaches your command(); the container's own names (start, stop, halt, goto, load, status, … — ./gerda ctl send describe lists them) never do, so give yours other names. ./gerda ctl get_state shows worker.status and, if the load failed, worker.fatal with the reason.

Inside tick you have the jsMacros service scope directly (World, Player, Hud, Java, …). This is enough for real behaviour; you trade type-safety and the mock test harness for zero ceremony. It uses only jsMacros' own API, so it runs on every Minecraft version and loader that has a jsMacros build (PORTABILITY.md).

Not this: ./gerda ctl load yourbot.js loads a passive side module into the container — a sandbox that sees only World/Player, runs next to the worker and never receives commands. It is not a way to run a bot.

docs.title: Recipe — a TS bot on the Runtime facade
docs.text:
One rung up: full TypeScript over the game, and — the real prize — a mock twin (src/core/runtime/mock.ts) that implements the identical Runtime interface, so your whole bot is unit-testable without Minecraft. This is the layer examples/advanced/standalone-bot.ts uses and nothing more.

The integration model is a fork — clone this repo as your workspace. There are deliberately no npm packages to depend on; the harness and the build assume they live in the tree with you.

  1. Write your entry anywhere in the tree, e.g. src/my-bot/entry.ts. It ends by assigning your Module onto the global: (globalThis as { Module?: unknown }).Module = makeYourBot(runtime);.
  2. Point the build at it — one line in tsup.config.ts: entry: { "__gerda_bot.bundle": "src/my-bot/entry.ts" }. worker.js loads the bundle by that fixed name, so building your entry under it is exactly how any custom bot replaces ours. Swap the line back to restore Gerda Bot.
  3. bun run build && ./gerda sync, then ./gerda reload-worker: the running worker keeps the old bundle until it reloads.
  4. Drive it: ./gerda ctl send <yourcmd> (a name the container does not own — start/stop/halt are container commands that manage the worker service). The just recipes wrap all of the above (just build, just sync, just watch).
  5. Test on the mock: construct your bot with createMockRuntime() (from src/core/runtime/mock.ts) instead of createJsMacrosRuntime() and assert against it — the facade is the seam that makes any bot on it testable, and it can't drift from the real runtime because both implement the same interface. Your tests go in test-ts/ and run under bun run check alongside ours.

docs.title: Using more of our stack
docs.text:
Once you're on the facade, pulling in kernel machinery is additive. The FSM + capability pipeline (src/shared/kernel/, src/bot/capabilities/), the navigator (src/shared/nav/), reflexes, and the mission sequencer are all separable modules — wire in the ones you want in your entry file. The graded worked examples walk each seam:

  • examples/intermediate/heartbeat-capability.ts — the smallest always-on capability (tick guard + typed blackboard slice + a command).
  • examples/advanced/patrol-mission.ts — a complete pluggable goal state-machine, the template every real mission follows.

The deep dive on missions/plans/capabilities and the Runtime contract is EXTENDING.md; the conventions reviews enforce are in CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Config overrides — tune without forking the schema
docs.text: Every tunable lives in one typed file (src/shared/config/schema.ts); a magic number in logic code is a bug. To change values for your deployment without editing that file, drop a gitignored config/local.overrides.json — a deep-partial override (e.g. { "nav": { "sprint": false } }) that makeConfig merges over the defaults at build time. It's validated: an unknown top-level key fails loud at init (naming the key + the file) rather than silently doing nothing. Details in EXTENDING.md.

docs.title: Your commands over the bridge & MCP — auto-discovery
docs.text: Add a describe() method to your Module and its entries merge into the container's command manifest (the mc://api resource). That means bridge_ctl, the MCP server, and any LLM operator discover your bot's commands with zero MCP redeploy — you ship a new bot, the manifest updates itself. Anything main.js doesn't handle itself falls through to your Module's command, reachable as ./gerda ctl send <type> or mc_send.

docs.title: Fleet — the hub is mission-agnostic
docs.text: Multi-bot coordination is not mining-specific. scripts/ops/fleet_hub.py queue entries are arbitrary {mission, params} mission_start payloads — enqueue your bot's missions with ./gerda fleet enqueue (or the mc_fleet_enqueue MCP tool) and the hub schedules them onto free bots with no hub changes. Only the small WANT_PRESETS dict (a resource → mission preset, "need iron" → a drill mission) and the vein-claim leasing semantics are mining-flavoured; ignore or replace them and the presence, disjoint-region, peers-as-obstacles, and task-queue machinery all still work. See FLEET_PLAYBOOK.md.

docs.title: A different pack or Minecraft version
docs.text: A plain-JS bot on jsMacros' own API runs on every version and loader that has a jsMacros build. Gerda Bot's raw-Java layer calls Forge SRG names: a different pack on Forge is mostly free, a Fabric or NeoForge runtime is a port. The tested support matrix and the porting steps are in PORTABILITY.md.

docs.title: Bridge command reference
docs.text:
Every command the bridge answers — 112 of them. Send one with ./gerda ctl send <name> '<json args>' or the mc_send MCP tool; a running bot serves the same set as the describe command and the mc://api MCP resource. Where two layers declare one name, the container row wins, as in dispatch (harness/main.js#buildManifest).

Arguments marked required must be present; the rest are optional. A command whose description starts with DIAG: is a diagnostic probe and is listed under Diagnostic instead of under its layer. The dispatch path behind the layers: IPC.md.

Command Layer Arguments Description greedy_drive worker x int requiredy int requiredz int required per-tick greedy nav to x/y/z (continuous veto; safe live test) — idle/paused only greedy_drive_stop worker — clear the per-tick greedy target + release keys greedy_stop worker — release the greedy navigator's movement keys (abort) greedy_to worker x int requiredy int requiredz int required drive one tick of the greedy navigator toward x/y/z — call repeatedly nav_trace worker tail int — return only the last N rows dump the un-sampled per-tick parkour trace of the last greedy_drive sensors worker items array — item ids to report stock forincludeStorage boolean — also count the open container's storage slots (default carry only) live read-out of the sustain-loop sensors — vein exhaustion + item stock (the cycle's guards) set_arrival worker dist number — e.g. 0.4 for exact-block runtime arrival tolerance for greedy_drive (≤0 clears → cfg.nav.gotoArrivalDist) set_dstar worker on bool — force the D* Lite incremental enginenoFiller bool — strip bridge/pillar/mine so D* engages per-drive engine override for greedy_drive A/B — D* Lite engine + strip filler moves set_timeout worker ticks number — e.g. 3000 (~150s) runtime timeout (ticks) for greedy_drive — raise for a long natural traverse (≤0 clears → cfg.nav.gotoTimeoutTicks) storage_probe worker x int requiredy int requiredz int required read a placed container's contents from the worker thread (kind/facing/slots) trace worker on bool — omit → report current state toggle per-tick decision tracing (T:TICK lines in get_logs) without a reload

docs.title: Extending Gerda Bot
docs.text: A practical guide to growing our reference bot (Gerda Bot): writing missions, plans, capabilities, and bridge commands, plus the SRG-mapping workflow for new jsMacros/Forge calls. Read this before adding a feature — it points you at the right layer and the existing patterns to copy. Writing your OWN bot on top of the harness instead — not extending ours? See Build your own bot.

docs.title: The two planes (pick the right one)
docs.text:
Mission plane (src/, bundled TS kernel) Primitive plane (harness/, jsMacros services) What Deterministic FSM: missions, capabilities, reflexes Bridge commands an operator (a script, you, or an LLM over MCP) calls directly over TCP Sees the world via the Runtime facade only (src/core/runtime/Runtime.ts) full jsMacros/Java (Java.type, Client, mod APIs) Can break/scan/move/place/use/craft/move-stacks (whatever the facade exposes) anything — screenshots, GUI clicks, EMI (Eyes & hands), jeval Can't call bridge primitives; touch raw Java run a tight per-tick control loop Add by a new mission/capability + bun run check a new ext.js plugin + reload_ext

Rule of thumb: a steady-state goal loop (mine until full, fell a tree) is a mission. A one-shot operator action (look up a recipe, click a GUI, drive a recipe book) is a primitive (ext.js / jeval). When the kernel needs a new world verb (place a block), add it to the facade (below) so missions can use it.

docs.title: Writing a mission
docs.text:
A Mission (src/shared/kernel/mission.ts) is a pluggable goal state-machine; the kernel runs ONE at a time, swapped at runtime via mission_start with no reload. The missions reference catalogs the shipped ones (params, outputs, phases); examples/advanced/patrol-mission.ts is a copy-ready hand-written template (examples/ is leveled basic → intermediate → advanced). Two ways to build one:

  • missionFromCaps(name, caps, opts) — compose from capability modules (handlers/ guards/edges/commands merged). Best when behavior splits into focused concerns. See src/bot/missions/mine/index.ts (scan/navigation/mine/loot/…). Caveat: the composed init does NOT receive mission_start params — use this only when config, not params, drives the mission.
  • Hand-written Mission object — when you need init(ctx, params). See src/bot/missions/fetch/index.ts (simplest), src/bot/missions/chop/index.ts (a full SCAN→GOTO→MINE loop), src/bot/missions/craft/index.ts (a stationary sub-stepped sequence).

A mission declares: - initialPhase + edges (a PartialTransitionTable<State> — only the phases it uses; GLOBAL_EDGES + UNIVERSAL_TARGETS are merged in by the kernel). - handlers: { PHASE(ctx) {…} } — one per phase it owns. - movementPhases — phases where the navigator drives motion (reflexes use this so they don't read the bot's own movement as human input). - init?(ctx, params), isDone?(ctx) (→ the sequencer decides what's next), outputs?(ctx) (data the next plan step can bind to), onAbort?(ctx). - optional guards (mission-scoped pre-dispatch middleware) and commands.

Steps to add one: 1. If it needs a new phase, add it to STATE in src/bot/profile/states.ts (like CRAFT/ RESTOCK) and list its edges in the mission's edges table. Mission-internal phases are NOT universal targets. 2. Keep per-mission scratch in a typed blackboard slice: defineSlice<T>("name", init) then ctx.slice(KEY). The global blackboard survives mission switches, so reset your slice in init (see resetChop). 3. Put pure logic in src/shared/domain/ (jsMacros-free, unit-tested); the handler only wires the facade to it. Tunables go in src/shared/config/schema.ts — a magic number in a handler is a bug. 4. Register it in src/bot/entry/worker-bundle.ts: .registerMission(myMission). 5. Test it on the mock in test-ts/ (drive kernel.tick(st); see chop-mission.test.ts for the GOTO-teleport + flushBreak loop pattern).

docs.title: Overriding config in a fork (without editing schema.ts)
docs.text: To tune tunables in a fork without touching src/shared/config/schema.ts, drop an OPTIONAL config/local.overrides.json — a deep-partial ConfigOverrides blob, e.g. { "nav": { "sprint": false } } — then rebuild. tsup bakes it into the bundle (esbuild define), and makeConfig merges it one level deep per section (siblings kept). The file is gitignored (per-fork, not shared); absent → the build is unchanged. An unknown top-level key fails loudly (a malformed/non-object file fails the BUILD; a valid JSON object with a bad section key throws a ContractError at bundle init, naming the key).

docs.title: Writing a plan (orchestrator)
docs.text:
A Plan (src/bot/orchestrator/plan.ts) is DATA: { name, steps, defaultMode? }, an ordered list of MissionSteps the orchestrator chains. This table is the complete step shape:

field meaning mission registered mission name; an unknown name parks the plan in failed params? a static object, or a ParamBinding (prev) => params that feeds the previous step's outputs into this one guards? StepGuardSpec[] checked before the step starts; a failing guard parks the plan in blocked (the reason shows in plan_status) mode? "auto" chains on completion; "approve" parks for a proceed/run command. Default: the plan's defaultMode, else "auto" id? label for select {step:"<id>"} jumps and for branch targets repeat? loop: run the step up to N times on success before advancing (default 1) repeatWhile? loop-until: a guard; re-run the step on success while it passes (overrides repeat) retries? retry: re-run the step up to N times when its mission ends in ERROR (default 0) next? branch on success: (prev) => id, index, null or undefined; null finishes the plan, undefined advances to the next step onFail? branch on failure: the step id/index to jump to once retries are spent; absent → the plan fails

Guards: src/bot/orchestrator/guards.ts (hasItems, inventoryHasRoom) and src/bot/orchestrator/sensors.ts (veinExhaustedGuard, lowStockGuard). Define plans in src/bot/plans/*.ts, register in worker-bundle.ts (makeOrchestrator(kernel, [myPlan])). Drive over the bridge: plan_start, proceed/continue, run, step, select, plan_status, plans, plan_abort.

The orchestrator is an always-on capability that also installs the kernel's MissionSequencer (src/shared/kernel/sequencer.ts) — the single hook consulted on mission completion. The default IDLE_SEQUENCER just goes IDLE; nothing else changes the single-active-mission invariant.

docs.title: Writing a capability
docs.text:
A Capability (src/shared/kernel/capability.ts) is a self-describing plugin: edges?, guard?(ctx) (pre-dispatch middleware; return true to short-circuit), handlers?, commands?, init?, requires? (resources resolved before its guard). Register ALWAYS-ON ones (lifecycle/reflexes/persistence/hud/telemetry/mission-control/ orchestrator) with kernel.register(cap) — they survive mission swaps. Set always: true for a heartbeat guard that runs even while idle (telemetry). Mission- scoped caps go through missionFromCaps. Reflexes live in src/shared/reflexes/ and only target universal landings (RECOVER/PAUSED/ERROR).

The always-on capabilities Gerda Bot registers, in makeModule() of src/bot/entry/worker-bundle.ts, after the reflexes (SAFETY.md). Each lives in src/bot/capabilities/ except the orchestrator (src/bot/orchestrator/index.ts); their commands are listed in COMMANDS.md.

Capability What it owns core The lifecycle commands start/pause/resume/halt and the shutdown teardown (keys released, Baritone stopped, HUD cleared). maintenance Resumable interrupts that suspend the exact phase and resume it (EAT). recover The RECOVER landing every reflex diverts to: release keys, teleport home, re-enter the mission. persistence Durable waypoints and run stats in mc_world.json; add_waypoint, remove_waypoint, save_now, goto_waypoint. hud The status overlay: phase, held-tool durability, waypoint and vein counters. telemetry Prometheus counters and gauges, pushed when cfg.telemetry.pushUrl is set; metrics. diagnostics The live facade smoke test, trace, storage_probe, and the one-tick greedy_to/greedy_stop. navProbe A per-tick greedy-navigator test drive while idle or paused: greedy_drive, nav_trace, set_arrival/set_dstar/set_timeout. navEngine nav_engine: the runtime navigator-engine override for production GOTO. sensors sensors: a read-out of what the sustain-loop guards see (vein exhaustion, item stock). event-export Mirrors the whitelisted bus events into the ring that poll_events drains. mission-control mission_start, mission_abort, mission_status, missions. chat-command In-game !<bot> <verb> driving; the trust list is off by default. orchestrator Chains missions into plans and installs the mission sequencer; the plan commands.

docs.title: Growing the harness (main.js / ext.js)
docs.text:
main.js is stable infra — rarely edited. New mod commands go in ext.js, the reloadable plugin layer. Each plugin self-registers:

register("my_cmd", function (req, id) {
  // req = the parsed JSON command; return a plain object (becomes the response data)
  return { ok: true, foo: 42 };
}, { where: "ext", desc: "one line: what it does", params: [{ name: "x", type: "int", required: true }] });

Globals available to plugins: Java, World, Player, Hud, Chat, Client, KeyBind, JavaWrapper, writeResp, register. Iteration loop: edit ext.js → ./gerda sync → reload_ext (re-evals into a fresh EXT registry, rollback-on-error, NO main restart). Removed/renamed commands disappear on reload. Each plugin carries its own "how this was derived" SRG/reflection comment. The meta is the command's row in COMMANDS.md: after adding or changing one, run just commands-ref.

To add a container meta-command (eyes/hands/eval-class), it goes in main.js HANDLERS; after editing + ./gerda sync, send reload_main (defers a restartService, so the response flushes first; the worker keeps running). A running main.js that does not know reload_main yet needs one bootstrap restart. Send this as jeval; the restart runs on a background thread, so the render thread never blocks:

new java.lang.Thread(JavaWrapper.methodToJava(function () {
  java.lang.Thread.sleep(1000);
  JsMacros.getServiceManager().restartService("main");
})).start()

After that restart, reload_main works.

docs.title: SRG-mapping workflow (calling vanilla/Forge methods)
docs.text:
Forge 1.20.1 obfuscates vanilla method names to SRG (m_6375_ etc.); jsMacros' wrapper classes are NOT remapped (call them by real name). So:

  • jsMacros-wrapped API (Player.getInteractionManager().interactBlock(...), Player.getPlayer().lookAt(...), World.getBlock(...)) → call by name, no SRG. Declare the method in types/jsmacros.d.ts so the facade can use it.
  • Raw vanilla Screen/client internals (GUI clicks, key events, recipe book) → need the SRG name. The runtime uses Mojang class names but SRG member names (LocalPlayer.respawn() is called as m_7583_, Options.keyUse is f_92095_). Find the name with these tools, in order:
  • scripts/dev/srg.py — offline name resolver (start here). Composes the launcher's on-disk mapping files (no download, no in-game risk):
    • srg.py LocalPlayer respawn → m_7583_ (Mojang member → SRG; lists overloads with descriptors; falls back to a global search if the member is inherited).
    • srg.py --rev m_7583_ → LocalPlayer.respawn() (SRG → Mojang).
    • srg.py --class FoodData → the class's full Mojang↔SRG table. With a ParchmentMC export present (mappings/parchment-*.json), lookups gain parameter names + javadoc: srg.py AbstractContainerMenu clicked → m_150399_ # …clicked(int slotId, int button, ClickType clickType, Player player). Parchment release 2023.09.03 is the final one for 1.20.1. Download it once into mappings/ (the srg.py docstring has the one-liner) and the index picks it up. Don't find a name by calling candidate m_…_ names in-game: the call runs on the render thread and can trip the EventLockWatchdog (and drop the world).
  • reflect {expr, filter?, depth?, mojang?} over the bridge (ext.js) — evaluate any expression and dump its runtime class's method signatures + fields, with each SRG name annotated with its Mojang name + Parchment param names (m_38707_(int,float):void →eat(foodLevelModifier, saturationLevelModifier) — runtime TYPES, Parchment NAMES) via srg_names.json (exported by srg.py --export, deployed by gerda sync). The live companion to srg.py: reflect {expr:"Player.openInventory()", filter:"craft"}, reflect {expr:"Java.type('dev.emi.emi.api.recipe.EmiRecipe')"}. mojang:false to skip.
  • Read the source when you need to know what a method does (not just its name): scripts/dev/decompile.sh mc (decompiles the MC client jar with Vineflower) or scripts/dev/decompile.sh mod <name> (any mod, e.g. emi/gtceu), then rg -n 'PATTERN' decompiled/…. The output is Mojang-named: SRG member tokens are rewritten through srg.py --remap (--raw keeps them SRG). Output is gitignored. Needs the flake dev shell (it provides vineflower + jdk21).
  • Signature on mappings.dev / Linkie under the owning class (web fallback), or cross-check the names already in main.js's SRG map. In src/, the one home for SRG tokens is src/core/runtime/jsmacros/srg.ts; add a new one there.
  • When even that won't reach it (obfuscated client internals jsMacros doesn't wrap, e.g. the recipe book): use a jeval bridge primitive with reflection, and prove it live with a probe (harness/probes/probe_runtime.js) BEFORE relying on it. Crafting is an example: the recipe-book API does not work on Monifactory, so the facade crafts through manual grid placement.

In jeval, don't paste raw SRG tokens (they rot on a version bump and read as noise). ext.js exposes a global srg(class, member) (and srgAll for overloads) that inverts srg_names.json, so you call vanilla methods by their Mojang name: var raw = Player.getPlayer().getRaw(); raw[srg('Player','getFoodData')]()[srg('FoodData','getFoodLevel')](). srg() throws if the name is unknown (fail-loud); inherited members resolve under their DECLARING class (srg('LivingEntity','getMainHandItem'), not the subclass). It reloads with reload_ext (same JS context as jeval).

Regenerate the reflect annotation map after a version change: python3 scripts/dev/srg.py --export harness/srg_names.json then just sync.

docs.title: The Runtime facade contract
docs.text:
src/core/runtime/Runtime.ts is the ONLY abstraction over jsMacros. Any new world verb: 1. add the method to the Runtime interface (Runtime.ts); 2. implement it for real in src/core/runtime/jsmacros/ (the ONLY code that touches the globals and the only place allowed try/catch, inside attempt/fx); 3. implement it in src/core/runtime/mock.ts (in-memory) — the build fails until you do, which is what keeps the mock from drifting; 4. declare any new jsMacros method it calls in types/jsmacros.d.ts.

Result<T> semantics: an err means a REAL external failure — never fabricate a fallback a caller could mistake for data. Callers branch on .ok (the defensive checker forbids dropping a Result). The interact group in Runtime.ts is a good example.

docs.title: The verify-convention (effect-check critical actions)
docs.text:
Result<T> is a contract on the call (it returns err on a real failure). It is NOT a contract on the effect — a fire-and-forget action can return ok yet not change the world (a bite the render thread dropped, a /home on cooldown, a deposit into a full chest). For the handful of irreversible / expensive / autonomy-critical actions, add a lightweight effect-check; do NOT build a framework or check every action (pure reads and cheap-to-retry writes don't need it).

The convention, in a tick-driven handler: 1. snapshot the relevant state before the action (food level, position, slot counts); 2. act; 3. once settled, read the state back and compare — emit an effect-verified event / log on success, and a WARN on the failure case (never proceed silently).

Worked examples (copy these): - maintenance.EAT — bites until player.food() ≥ target, emits ate; WARNs EAT_TIMEOUT / EAT_OUT_OF_FOOD when food does not rise. - recover.RECOVER — presses respawn until player.alive(), emits respawned. - home-return.HOME/RETURN — snapshots XZ, then WARNs TELEPORT_NO_MOVE if the player didn't move ≥ cfg.teleportMinMoveBlocks, so a failed /home never proceeds at the wrong spot. - storage.DUMP — re-reads the bag after depositing and WARNs DEPOSIT_INCOMPLETE if ore remains, so a full chest shows up in the log instead of looping. - craft — takes the server-computed yield (craft.take() returns the real count) and isDone checks the inventory count reached the goal.

The live smoke harness (diagnostics.ts) is the build-time companion: it exercises the raw-Java facade methods in the worker context so a broken effect path is caught by scripts/ops/facade_smoke.py before a real run, not mid-combat.

docs.title: Reliability rules (enforced by bun run check)
docs.text: bun run check = tsc + biome + vitest + check-defensive. The defensive checker forbids, outside designated boundaries: try/catch, as casts, empty catches, dropped Results. The versioned git hooks (just hooks) run it as the gate; what each hook runs: TESTING.md. Escape hatch: a // reliability-ok: <reason> comment on the line (used e.g. for the orchestrator's plan-input boundary, since it dispatches as owner=core and a bad plan must not become a CoreFatalError). Prefer must() / a type guard over a cast.

docs.title: Bundle size budget
docs.text:
scripts/ops/sync.py refuses to deploy a bundle longer than MAX_CODE_LEN characters (just validate-bundle and the pre-push hook run the same check). It is a review budget, not a runtime limit: worker.js eval-loads the bundle with no length check, and GraalJS evaluates far larger code. The budget exists so that bundle growth is a decision someone writes down. The comment above MAX_CODE_LEN lists every raise and what it paid for.

The budget is 1 MiB (1048576 characters); the full Gerda Bot bundle is about 592000, so a fork has roughly 450000 characters of room for its own capabilities and missions. just validate-bundle prints <size>/<budget>. When your change goes over, either trim it or raise MAX_CODE_LEN and add one line to that comment naming what grew. The separate 256000 cap in harness/main.js limits the snippets the eval bridge command accepts; it does not apply to the bundle.

docs.title: Deploy / verify loop
docs.text:
• just build / bun run build — tsup → dist/__gerda_bot.bundle.js (IIFE).
  • just sync / bun run deploy — build + deploy bundle + services to game instances.
  • Kernel/bundle change → full redeploy (worker re-evals the bundle). ext.js change → reload_ext. main.js change → reload_main.
  • Inspect a live bot via the mc MCP tools (mc_ping/mc_get_state/mc_send) or python scripts/ops/bridge_ctl.py … (also ./gerda ctl …, the repo-root umbrella CLI that dispatches to the scripts/ops+scripts/dev tools). Use get_logs to read the NDJSON journal between steps (e.g. ORCH_*, MISSION_*, LOG_FOUND, CRAFT_*).

docs.title: Eyes & hands: screenshots and GUI input
docs.text:
The harness lets you see the game and work its menus over the bridge. You can take a screenshot, read it, click a button, scroll a list and type into a text field. Nothing needs the mouse, the keyboard or even a visible window. This page is for a developer or an LLM operator who drives a client through ./gerda ctl or the mc_send MCP tool.

All commands below are container commands in harness/screen.js, plus the EMI commands in harness/ext.js. ./gerda ctl send <type> '<json>' sends any of them from a shell. From MCP, use mc_send with the same type and payload. To reach a bot client instead of the default port, add --port <port> or --bot <name> before send.

docs.title: Take one
docs.text:
./gerda ctl send screenshot                     # writes <instance>/minecraft/screenshots/ai_shot.png
./gerda ctl send screenshot '{"name": "a.png"}' # any other file name

The command calls jsMacros Player.takeScreenshot on the render thread. It captures the game's own framebuffer, so it sees every GUI, including custom-rendered ones (FTB Quests, GregTech machine screens). The file is overwritten on every call.

The reply comes back before the file is written. Wait about a second before you read it, or compare mtime from latest_screenshot (path and modification time of the newest PNG).

Off-screen frames need enableVsync:false

Set enableVsync:false in the instance's options.txt. With vsync on, a window that is hidden, minimized or off-screen stops rendering, and every screenshot shows the same stale frame.

docs.title: Read one
docs.text:
./gerda shot (= python3 scripts/ops/mc_shot.py) resizes and crops a shot into one output file, /tmp/mc_shot.png by default:

./gerda shot --file -s 0.4                     # ai_shot.png, scaled to 40%
./gerda shot --file -g "730,320 1100x800"      # one region, full resolution
./gerda shot --file a.png -s 0.5 -o out.png    # another file, another output path
./gerda shot --latest                          # newest PNG in screenshots/ (e.g. an F2 press)
Flag Meaning --file [NAME] Read screenshots/NAME (default ai_shot.png). --latest Read the newest PNG in screenshots/. -s SCALE Downscale factor (default 0.5). -g "X,Y WxH" Crop a region, in full-resolution pixels. The crop runs before the scale. -o OUT Output path (default /tmp/mc_shot.png).

The file modes need ffmpeg. By default they read the human instance named by humanInstance in local.config.json. To read a bot or camera client, point MC_INST at that instance's minecraft directory (an absolute path). Without it you get the human instance's old ai_shot.png, not the frame you just took:

MC_INST=/path/to/instances/<bot instance>/minecraft ./gerda shot --file -s 0.33

Without --file or --latest, mc_shot.py grabs the visible window from the desktop instead. That mode is optional and works only on a niri (Wayland) session with grim. The in-game screenshot command plus --file works everywhere.

docs.title: Keep the cost down (LLM operators)
docs.text:
An image costs tokens by its pixel count, not its file size. JPEG does not help. On a window about 2560 pixels wide:

Shot Approx. tokens -s 0.5 1,200 -s 0.33 530 -s 0.25 300 tight -g crop 100

Take a small overview first. Then crop the part you need at full resolution.

Before you take a screenshot at all, ask whether a data command answers the question. read_screen lists a vanilla screen's buttons. emi_search returns item ids. The FTB quest files sit on disk. Each is cheaper than an image.

docs.title: Coordinates
docs.text:
There are two coordinate systems:

  • Framebuffer pixels. The screenshot is the full framebuffer, so its size is the game window's size in pixels (for example 2544×1392). It is not your monitor's size.
  • GUI coordinates. These are what click and scroll take. A GUI coordinate is a framebuffer pixel divided by the GUI scale.
gui_x = framebuffer_x / guiScale
gui_y = framebuffer_y / guiScale

Set an explicit guiScale in options.txt (our instances use 4). With 0 (auto), the scale changes with the window size. Minecraft also lowers the scale when the window is too small for it: scale n needs a window of at least 320·n × 240·n pixels, so 4 needs 1280×960.

Convert from the image you actually read:

  • A shot taken with -s s shows pixel p for framebuffer pixel p / s.
  • A shot cropped with -g "X,Y WxH" is offset: framebuffer x = X + p / s, y = Y + p / s.

Example: a downscaled shot (-s 0.5) shows a button at (424, 280). That is framebuffer (848, 560), so you click GUI (212, 140) at guiScale:4.

docs.title: Hands: GUI input
docs.text:
Command Payload What it does read_screen — Title and button widgets (i, text, x, y, w, h, active) of the open screen; open:false in the world. click {i} or {text} Click a standard button by index or by a label substring. click {x, y, button?} Mouse click at GUI coordinates. button 0 = left (default), 1 = right. scroll {x, y, amount?} Scroll at GUI coordinates. Positive is up, negative is down; default -3. type {text} Type text into the focused widget. Click the text field first. keypress {code, scancode?, mods?} Send a GLFW key to the open screen: Enter 257, Backspace 259, Escape 256, Tab 258, arrows 262–265. key {key, hold?, release?} Tap a named keybind (key.inventory, key.use, key.drop). hold:true keeps it down until a release:true call. close_screen — Close the open screen. introspect {target?, filter?} Debug: list method names on the jsMacros libraries, or on the open screen with target:"screen". 
./gerda ctl send read_screen
./gerda ctl send click '{"text": "Done"}'
./gerda ctl send click '{"x": 212, "y": 140}'
./gerda ctl send scroll '{"x": 212, "y": 140, "amount": -5}'
./gerda ctl send type '{"text": "iron"}'
./gerda ctl send keypress '{"code": 257}'

click, scroll, type and keypress call the real vanilla Screen methods (mouseClicked/mouseReleased, mouseScrolled, charTyped, keyPressed/keyReleased). They run on the render thread, so the reply means "scheduled", not "done". Take a screenshot to see the result. At runtime Forge exposes these methods only under their SRG names; the harness keeps that table, and Extending § SRG-mapping workflow explains it.

read_screen sees standard widgets only. A custom-rendered GUI reports open:true, an empty title and no buttons. Use a screenshot there.

docs.title: Which GUIs accept synthetic input
docs.text:
GUI Synthetic click / scroll / type What to do Vanilla screens: containers, buttons, anvil and sign text fields Yes Use the commands above. FTB Library screens, such as the FTB Quests book Yes, at the coordinates you pass Click quest nodes and scroll the tree directly. EMI or JEI overlays: the item list and its search bar No Use the emi_* commands below.

Vanilla and FTB Library screens take the coordinates from the call. They need no OS cursor and no window focus. EMI and JEI hit-test the real OS cursor and read the keyboard below the screen, so synthetic events never reach them.

docs.title: EMI as data
docs.text:
EMI's classes keep their real names on Forge, so harness/ext.js calls its Java API directly.

Command Payload Result emi_search {text, limit?} Matching item ids as data, for example results: ["minecraft:iron_ingot", …]. limit defaults to 60. emi_recipe {item} Opens the recipe screen for what crafts the item. emi_uses {item} Opens the recipe screen for where the item is used. 
./gerda ctl send emi_search '{"text": "@gtceu raw"}'
./gerda ctl send emi_recipe '{"item": "minecraft:iron_ingot"}'

emi_search needs no screen, no screenshot and no focus. It accepts the full EMI query syntax (@mod, #tag, tooltip text). It waits about 8 ticks for EMI's background search, then reads the result. It also leaves your text in EMI's search bar. Use it to find out which items exist instead of reading the item panel from an image.

emi_recipe and emi_uses open a screen. Read it with a screenshot, then close_screen.

docs.title: FTB Quests
docs.text:
The quest book is an FTB Library screen. click and scroll work on it, and read_screen is blind to it. Read the quest tree from disk instead of from screenshots:

  • <instance>/minecraft/config/ftbquests/quests/chapters/*.snbt holds the quest ids, x/y grid positions, dependencies, task type and items.
  • Title keys such as {moni.quest.*} and {moni.task.*} resolve through <instance>/minecraft/kubejs/assets/ftbquests/lang/en_us.json. Other packs keep their own lang file.

A checkmark task completes when you click it. An item task completes when the player holds the item. To read quest state and to complete or claim quests without the GUI, use the bridge commands in Fleet playbook § FTB Quests.

docs.title: A reliable loop
docs.text:
1. screenshot, then ./gerda shot --file -s 0.33 for an overview.
  2. Crop tightly around the target with -g at full resolution, and find its centre.
  3. Convert the centre to framebuffer pixels, then divide by guiScale.
  4. click {x, y}.
  5. screenshot again and check that the screen changed the way you expected.

Repeat from step 1 when it did not. A click that lands but does nothing usually means the coordinates are off by the scale factor, or the screen is an EMI or JEI overlay.

docs.title: Fleet playbook — playing alongside the bots
docs.text: How to drive the co-op fleet on the dedicated server: the server rules, fleet and chat control, FTB Quests, and prospector charging. For adding missions and plugins see EXTENDING.md.

docs.title: 1. The server and how the bots play (read first)
docs.text:
Dedicated server: <server-root>/monifactory-<version>/, controlled with ./server-ctl.sh {start|stop|cmd|status|log} (SERVER_SETUP.md).

  • In fleet play, each bot plays like a real player: no cheats, no handouts. Bots (bot_1..bot_N) are not op; only your own account <your-account> is. Keep it that way — hand-feeding a bot items bypasses the economy the bot is built to run.
  • Teleport is the bots' one privilege: FTB Essentials /home, /back, /spawn, /rtp (FTB Essentials does not op-gate these by default; check its config). The bot's own recovery uses /home and /back (src/bot/missions/mine/home-return.ts, homeCommand/backCommand in src/shared/config/schema.ts). Give every bot its home once, on a safe spot: ./gerda ctl send chat '{"message": "/sethome base"}'. Without it, /home base answers Unknown destination! and the bot does not move. After cfg.safety.homeNoEffectLimit such recovery sends in a row, each from a spot away from the bot's recorded home, the bot stops sending /home and logs HOME_COMMAND_DISABLED (the server kicks a non-op player who repeats commands too fast). A bot with no recorded home yet (it records one only where the mine mission's HOME leg /home moved it) counts every such send. It sends again cfg.safety.homeRearmTicks later, or at once after a chat home. Keep the /home cooldown at 0 (SERVER_SETUP § 4).
  • Scaffolding goes through the server console or your op account: ./server-ctl.sh cmd "setblock …", cmd "give <your-account> …", cmd "tp bot_N x y z". Arena and film-set builds (scripts/dev/arena.py) need an op client: your op account, or a test bot opped for one just gate-live session and de-opped after.
  • Server settings: always day (doDaylightCycle=false), difficulty peaceful (no hunger, no hostile mobs), online-mode=false, enforce-secure-profile=false, no whitelist (trusted LAN). Generate a fresh world with a random seed on first setup.

docs.title: 2. Driving the fleet
docs.text:
• Names. target= and registry names are instance dirs (Monifactory_bot_1…); in-game and console names are bot_1….
  • Tools. The mc_* tools come from the mc MCP server; wire it once (SETUP.md § Wire the MCP server). Every MCP call has a shell equivalent: ./gerda ctl --bot <instance> … for one bot, ./gerda fleet … for the hub.
  • One bot: mc_send / mc_get_state / mc_ping with target=Monifactory_bot_N, or ./gerda ctl --bot Monifactory_bot_N status. Talks to that bot's bridge directly; no hub needed.
  • Fleet state: mc_fleet_status / mc_fleet_map / mc_fleet_claims / mc_fleet_assign / mc_fleet_unassign need the coordinator hub: ./gerda hub (scripts/ops/fleet_hub.py, port 8849). Track its PID; do not pkill -f fleet_hub (the pattern can match your own shell and kill it). From a shell, ./gerda fleet status|map|claims|queue|want|enqueue|cancel|assign|unassign talks to the same hub:

./gerda hub --http 127.0.0.1:8849 --interval 2.0          # the hub (a daemon; keep it running)
./gerda fleet want iron --bots 2                          # two bots drill iron
./gerda fleet enqueue drill '{"ore":"iron"}' --bot Monifactory_bot_2 --ttl 1800
./gerda fleet assign Monifactory_bot_1 -520 -460 -380 -320  # region lease: minX maxX minZ maxZ
- Regions keep two bots off one vein: mc_fleet_assign {bot, allowed:{minX,maxX,minZ,maxZ}}. The hub pushes each bot its allowed box plus forbidden = the peers' boxes (mc_assignment). The assignment has no TTL — always mc_fleet_unassign. - Task queue — say what you need; free bots pick it up: curl -X POST localhost:8849/fleet/enqueue -d '{"mission":"drill","params":{"ore":"iron"}}'. Optional "bot":"Monifactory_bot_2" pins it, "ttl":1800 bounds it; without bot the first free bot takes it (FIFO). Only online, IDLE, untasked fleet instances are dispatched: *_bot_* names, plus the instances listed in local.config.json "fleetInstances": ["Monifactory"] (env MC_FLEET_INSTANCES). Any other instance counts as the human's own client and gets no task. On the one-instance setup of SETUP.md, list Monifactory there, or the queue never runs; while no fleet instance is online, enqueue and want reply with a warning that says so. Outcome is read from the bot: finished run = done; PAUSED = done and aborted; ERROR = failed and aborted; bot offline = bounded requeue; TTL as backstop. GET /fleet/queue lists, POST /fleet/cancel {id} cancels. The queue persists in mc-tasks.json. MCP: mc_fleet_enqueue / mc_fleet_queue / mc_fleet_cancel. - Want presets — ask for a resource: curl -X POST localhost:8849/fleet/want -d '{"resource":"iron"}' enqueues the mission that produces it (bots:N fans out, bot: pins, ttl: bounds). Ore words → drill {ore} (prospect → shaft → mine); wood → chop; food → hunt (WANT_PRESETS in fleet_hub.py). Unknown words become drill {ore:<word>}, which skips gracefully if no vein is found. MCP: mc_fleet_want.

docs.title: 2.0 Driving a bot from in-game chat
docs.text:
A player near the bots can drive them from chat — no bridge, no MCP:

!<botname|all> <verb> [args…]      e.g.  !bot_2 goto 120 70 -40      !all pause
  • Addressing. !bot_2 … reaches the bot named bot_2 (case-insensitive); !all … reaches every bot in earshot. Lines for other bots are ignored; a bot never acts on its own output.
  • Verbs: status, pause, resume, stop/abort, home, mine, drill [ore], chop [n], hunt [n], goto <x> <y> <z>, follow <player>. Each routes through the same commands as the bridge, so the reply reports what actually happened (failed: … on a no-op). home stops movement and the mission, then sends the cfg.homeCommand teleport, also when the bot had disabled it after HOME_COMMAND_DISABLED. Numbers must be whole decimals within chat.maxCoordXZ / minCoordY / maxCoordY / maxCount; chop -5, goto 0x10 70 0 and surplus args are refused with a reply.
  • Trust. cfg.chat.trustedPlayers in src/shared/config/schema.ts is empty by default, which admits nobody. The shipped pack profile (src/bot/profile/pack.ts) sets ["*"] (anyone) for a private, peaceful, offline-mode server. On a shared server list your own names: chat: { trustedPlayers: ["Alex", "…"] }. Matching is exact and case-sensitive. This is not authentication — on an offline-mode server anyone can log in under any name. Untrusted lines addressed by name get one refusal per sender per chat.denyReplyTicks; untrusted broadcasts are logged, never answered.
  • Replies start with cfg.chat.replyPrefix ([gerda]), so a reply never parses as a command. The home teleport is sent verbatim.
  • Troubleshooting. Chat is queued on the listener thread (bounded by chat.queueCapacity, drop-oldest) and handled on the tick thread. The parser expects vanilla <Name> text; on a server that decorates chat, look for CHAT_NO_PARSE in get_logs. If nothing shows, lower the log level (trace) and look for CHAT_SELF (DBG): it proves the bot hears chat; its absence means the listener never fired.

docs.title: 2.1 Launching, relaunching and reconnecting a bot
docs.text:
Four levels of restart — use the lightest that works:

  • reload_ext — re-evaluates ext.js (mod-API plugins).
  • reload_main — re-reads main.js headlessly; the worker keeps running.
  • reload_worker — restarts the worker (kernel + bundle) off-thread: ./gerda reload-worker (scripts/ops/reload_worker.py). It dials the same bridge as ./gerda ctl: --port or --bot, else MC_BRIDGE_PORT, else 55544. Do not send a bare halt to a stuck worker: it blocks main.js's tick and the whole bridge goes deaf. Example: ./gerda reload-worker --bot Monifactory_bot_1 --timeout 60. On an ack timeout it reports and does not retry; check ./gerda ctl --bot Monifactory_bot_1 status before you send it again. If one worker tick runs for minutes (a CPU-starved client, software rendering), the reload waits behind it. Then ./gerda ctl restart_service worker stops the worker from bridge.js and leaves it stopped; ./gerda ctl start starts it again. get_state.worker.tickPace counts the slow ticks.
  • Cold JVM launch — full client restart, for a crashed or wedged client or a new account binding. Launch and join in one launcher command (adjust for your launcher):
freesmlauncher -l Monifactory_bot_1 -s localhost:25565 -a bot_1

-l instance dir, -s host:port joins on launch, -a offline account. Stop the old client first (kill -TERM <javaPID>; find it by -Djava.library.path=…/instances/<inst>/natives in ps). Ports: ./gerda sync assigns each instance a bridge port from 55544 up, keeps it across deploys and records it in mc-bots.json. A cold boot starts the worker in IDLE once the world loads; survival reflexes are always on, no start needed. - Reconnect after a disconnect screen. Drive it headless: click{i:0} → Multiplayer → click "Direct Connection" → click "Join Server" (the address field keeps the last host). A relog returns the player to where it logged out; if that spot is unsafe, move it from the console (server-ctl.sh cmd "tp bot_N x y z"). - Keep-alive timeouts. A freshly booted modded client can stall past the server's keep-alive window if loaded hard at once (bulk /fill, teleports into loading chunks). Let chunks settle 10–20 s after boot.

docs.title: 3. FTB Quests (read, complete, claim)
docs.text:
The bot drives FTB Quests through its native API — no GUI or screenshots.

  • Read the tree from disk: ids, grid positions, dependencies, task type and items live in $INST/config/ftbquests/quests/chapters/*.snbt; title keys ({moni.quest.*}, {moni.task.*}) resolve via $INST/kubejs/assets/ftbquests/lang/en_us.json. $INST = <instances-root>/Monifactory/minecraft; ./gerda config instances_root prints the root.
  • Live state and actions (ext.js bridge commands):
  • quests {…} — quest and task state from ClientQuestFile.
  • count_item {…} — how many of an item the bot holds.
  • quest_complete {…} — mutating: submits task(s) via SubmitTaskMessage. Item tasks need the item in inventory (not consumed when consume_items=false); checkmark tasks complete on submit.
  • quest_claim {…} — mutating: claims only the named quest's rewards (ClaimRewardMessage per reward).
  • Quest and reward ids are 16-hex unsigned longs: java.lang.Long.parseUnsignedLong(hex,16).
  • Autopilot: scripts/objective/ (mod-agnostic; FTB adapter in sources/ftb_quests.py) runs multi-step chains behind an approve-each gate. Use the raw commands for one-offs. Needs a running bot; preview first, then approve one quest:
./gerda objective --dry-run --chapter genesis   # next objective + its plan, mutates nothing
./gerda objective --once --chapter genesis      # asks, then acts on at most one quest

--chapter takes a chapter file name from chapters/*.snbt, --quest <16-hex id> targets one quest, and --mode auto --allow-mine runs unattended with the mining tier on. - Item tasks detect the item when the bot holds it: the bot mines or crafts the item, holds it, then quest_complete.

docs.title: 4. Charging the prospector
docs.text:
The HV prospector runs on EU and is charged the way a player charges it:

  • A Turbo Charger (quest "Charging Items", id 06E9B9DDDB245F38) charges RF and EU. The Tinker's Workstation and Wireless Charger are RF-only and do not charge it.
  • prospector_status reads the stored charge (lowPct threshold, default 15 %). When the prospector is empty, prospecting reports "out of energy" and the drill pauses instead of failing. Put the prospector in the charger, then run prospect and resume. Operating GTCEu machines is the player's part of the co-op — the bot runs the basic vanilla economy.

docs.title: 5. Seeing players and peers
docs.text:
The mob feed (publishMobs) excludes players. Players and other bots come from a separate feed:

  • mc_peers — main.js publishes player positions, worker.js mirrors them to __MC_PEERS, and the facade exposes world.peers(). The follow mission uses it.
  • Peers are obstacles — the planner treats columns near peers as blocked (cfg.nav.peerObstacle, rebuilt from world.peers() every plan); the goal column is exempt, so follow can still walk to a peer.
  • One-off scouting without a mission: poll ./server-ctl.sh cmd "data get entity <name> Pos" and push a greedy_drive target every few ticks.

docs.title: 6. Coordination features
docs.text:
• Vein claims — the hub reads each bot's drill target (mission_status → drill.vein) and leases vein:x,z for it (TTL 90 s, renewed per poll). Peers skip veins within cfg.fleetVeinClaimRadius (8) of another bot's claim (DRILL_CLAIM_SKIP).
  • Shared hazards — each bot records ravines and drowned columns in mc_world.json hazards. The hub merges them per dimension and pushes assignment.hazards to every bot, so one bot's hazard is avoided by all.
  • Pushes go only to region-claimed bots and online *_bot_* instances (never the human's client) and are skipped when unchanged. Offline tests: test-ts/fleet-coordination.test.ts.
  • Live gate: just gate-live runs every asserting arena plus the navigator benches with one exit code (--quick = core set). It needs a live opped test bot, so you run it locally by hand (TESTING.md).

docs.title: Bridge transport & IPC contract
docs.text: How the three plain-JS jsMacros services (bridge.js / main.js / worker.js) talk to each other and to host tooling — the TCP transport, the GlobalVars key namespace, and the command envelope. Every key and every wire shape is defined once in harness/ipc.js (the SSOT), mirrored to src/core/ipc/ipc.ts for the worker bundle; drift between the two fails bun run check (test-ts/ipc-contract.test.ts).
