  2. Add Oculus to its mods/ and a shaderpack to its shaderpacks/, and enable the pack in config/oculus.properties (shaderPack=…, enableShaders=true).

  3. Give it the camera's account and bridge port (set its port in mc-bots.json to the camera's). It replaces the camera: never boot both, and pass --skip <shader-instance> to a sync while it runs.

  4. Keep enableVsync:false (every rig instance): with vsync on, an off-screen window stops rendering.

  5. Read the frame rate: python3 scripts/ops/bridge_ctl.py --port <camera-port> send jeval '{"code":"Client.getMinecraft()[srg(\"Minecraft\",\"getFps\")]()"}'.
  6. Screenshots: MC_INST=<instances>/<shader-instance>/minecraft python3 scripts/ops/mc_shot.py --file -s 0.4.

docs.title: Sets — restage the world from data
docs.text:
A film set is staged scenery stored as data: the arena spec format without a mission.

scenarios/arenas/<name>.json   ops + mission + expect   → `just gate-live` runs these
scenarios/sets/<name>.json     ops + snapshot, no mission → staging only, never in the gate

Shipped sets: 03_ore_chamber (shots 03_vein, 02b_shaft; carries the drill marker), 04b_gap (shot 04b), 02_mesa_clutch (shot 01_clutch). A set that declares mission/plan/expect is refused.

python3 scripts/dev/arena.py list                                          # arenas + sets
python3 scripts/dev/arena.py snapshot sets/03_ore_chamber --port 55546     # live world → ops
python3 scripts/dev/arena.py build    sets/03_ore_chamber --port 55546     # data → world
python3 scripts/dev/arena.py clean    sets/03_ore_chamber --port 55546     # back to air
  • Keys: SCENARIOS.md § Film sets.
  • Always pass --port. The default, 55544, is the human's instance.
  • Spec shape. snapshot.boxes is the input; ops_generated is written by snapshot — never by hand. Hand-written setup (marker, give, player, select, wait) goes in ops. build applies ops_generated, then ops.
  • Snapshot before you change the world; a set restores only what was captured. Capture is 1:1 including air, by block id only: stairs and slabs restage in default orientation, so put them in ops. Oversized boxes, bad reads, unloaded chunks and builds over 2000 ops abort.
  • build needs an op client (chat /fill, /setblock): drive it from the camera, or op a test bot for the session and de-op after. It re-reads a sub-box and aborts on a mismatch.
  • snapshot needs loaded chunks, no fluids in the box (a fluid restages as a permanent source), and stamps the dimension; build refuses a client in another dimension.
  • marker writes the world store of the instance in MC_INST (default: human). For a drill target: MC_INST=<instances>/Monifactory_bot_1/minecraft python3 scripts/dev/arena.py build sets/03_ore_chamber --port 55546.

docs.title: Edit — cut list → deliverable
docs.text:
scenarios/shots/<name>.json is the shoot half; <name>_cut.json is the edit half (take, in/out, speed, reason). scripts/rig/assemble.py cuts the film in one ffmpeg call:

python3 scripts/rig/assemble.py scenarios/shots/teaser_cut.json --dry-run     # command + durations
python3 scripts/rig/assemble.py scenarios/shots/teaser_cut.json               # cut it
python3 scripts/rig/assemble.py scenarios/shots/teaser_cut.json --only vein,finale

Segments are trimmed (optional speed, per-segment filters), normalised to the list's width/height/fps, concatenated and faded, with encode.sh's delivery settings. A missing take, an out past the source, out <= in, an unknown --only id or a bad speed aborts.

Captions (captions.cues[]) anchor to a segment (seg, at/dur in output seconds). Layers: label (caps tag, top left) and line (narrative, bottom third). They render to <out>.en.ass and are burned in. Readability limits live in assemble.py (MIN_HOLD_S, MAX_LINE, MAX_CPS) and abort the cut. Write a segment's speed as {speed}, not a typed 3×; write sizes unspaced (3×3). Fonts must resolve in fc-match.

Measure every in/out on the take (ffmpeg -ss <t> -i take.mp4 -frames:v 1 f.png, or the static runs from motion_probe.py) and put the reason in the segment's note.

docs.title: Showcase and console cards
docs.text: scenarios/shots/showcase.json and showcase_cut.json are a second shoot/edit pair: one goal-driven chain from a worn stone pickaxe to a crafted iron one, then the live gate. Its in/out values are placeholders until the takes are measured, and its _doc blocks list the shoot-day order and the poses still to measure. The two console inserts are takes rendered by scripts/rig/console_card.py from scenarios/shots/cards/*.json at the cut's size and fps. A number that only a run can give is a <FILL:name> token copied from that run: a render with an unfilled token aborts, and --draft previews the layout. The gate card is the literal all-PASS summary of the default gate set. It carries from_log, so its render needs --log with the log of a real run and refuses unless that log prints the same lines, the [gate] N/M passed line included. The script's docstring holds the spec schema; it needs the capture devShell (ffmpeg, fontconfig).

docs.title: Run — one client, headless, no camera
docs.text:
Commands and missions: FLEET_PLAYBOOK.md, EXTENDING.md.

Run the launcher once with a display first and finish its first-run wizard (language, account). A headless launch stops on that wizard and never boots the game; under a C locale the language page comes back every start until Language=en_US is set in the launcher's freesmlauncher.cfg.

# boot one client, keep-alive, no recording (drop -s for single-player)
nix develop .#capture -c scripts/ops/capture_rig.sh -a bot_1 -l Monifactory_bot_1 -s localhost:25565 -K &
python3 scripts/ops/bridge_ctl.py --port 55545 --wait-ready 120 status

# drive it (or the `mc` MCP tools: mc_get_state / mc_send / mc_fleet_*)
python3 scripts/ops/bridge_ctl.py --port 55545 get_state
python3 scripts/ops/bridge_ctl.py --port 55545 send mission_start '{"name":"mine"}'   # or plan_start '{"name":"sustain-cycle"}'

# see its screen, read from THAT instance
python3 scripts/ops/bridge_ctl.py --port 55545 send screenshot
MC_INST=$(python3 scripts/local_config.py instances_root)/Monifactory_bot_1/minecraft \
  python3 scripts/ops/mc_shot.py --file -s 0.4

scripts/rig/teardown.sh Monifactory_bot_1

get_logs tails a file. For live progress read the worker journal (…/Macros/miner.ndjson) and check its mtime.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Capture through headless sway. gamescope → PipeWire records black on the NVIDIA driver.
  • Run the client under Xwayland. The modded client crashes on native Wayland.
  • The headless output must be @60Hz, or it emits no frame callbacks and records one frame.
  • Never pkill -f / pgrep -f an instance name — it matches your own shell and kills it (exit 144). Use scripts/rig/teardown.sh. To list or count clients use scripts/rig/mc_clients.sh [instance] (… | grep -c . counts).
  • Furnace input caps at 64; smelt-load fails if it cannot load the whole stack. sustain_live.py loop empties each furnace per lap.
  • Hide the HUD on the camera; sustain_live.py frame does it and warns loudly if it cannot.

docs.title: Relocating the scene
docs.text: The sustain-cycle plan targets the furnace bank at cfg.sustain.basePos = {5,101,1} (src/bot/profile/pack.ts, compiled into the bundle). To film elsewhere, change basePos, rebuild, redeploy, and set ANCHOR in sustain_live.py. ANCHOR=(0,0,0) equals the arena fixture.

docs.title: Safety architecture — prevention / reaction / recovery
docs.text:
The bot's self-preservation is three concerns that cannot overlap by construction. When you add a mission or a guard, decide which tier it belongs to — putting one concern in the wrong tier is what creates conflicts and dead code.

Tier Owns the question Scope When it runs Where it lives Prevention "Will I choose to commit to something fatal?" self-movement / self-actions only plan-time planner (shared/domain/planner.ts, movement-types.ts), mission-specific guards (e.g. drill floorVerdict) Reaction "Is something hurting me right now?" any cause, incl. external (OP /tp, mob, lava) every tick the reflex layer (shared/reflexes/) Recovery "Get to safety + respawn" terminal landing on a reflex divert / death bot/capabilities/recover.ts (the RECOVER phase)

Prevention is plan-time & self-only; reaction is runtime & cause-agnostic; recovery is the landing every reaction diverts to. A given piece of logic belongs to exactly one.

docs.title: The rule that prevents duplicated dead code
docs.text:
Missions may PREVENT (proactive, task-specific), but must NOT re-implement REACTION.

  • ✅ The drill refusing to open a shaft floor over water or a fatal drop (floorVerdict in bot/missions/drill/floor-safety.ts) is Prevention — task-specific, stays in the mission. It is a different concern from the global swimOut / waterClutch reflexes (the reaction if prevention fails). That is defense-in-depth, not duplication.
  • ❌ A mission with its own if (health < X) teleport() would duplicate the vitals reflex — that is dead Reaction. Delete it and let vitals own it (the tool reflex owns worn tools).

If you catch yourself writing a health/air/fall reaction inside a mission, stop — it belongs in a reflex, where it runs for every mission and for the idle bot too.

docs.title: Reaction tier: survival vs mission-progress reflexes
docs.text:
Reflexes run before mission logic each tick, first-to-fire preempts. They split by an explicit survival flag on the capability (shared/kernel/capability.ts):

  • survival: true — life-preservation. Runs even when no mission is active (a parked/IDLE bot must not bleed out), via the kernel's idle survival pass. Members: death (respawn), air + swimOut (don't drown), waterClutch (survive falls), vitals (HP floor + distress). If one diverts, RECOVER runs in the idle path too, so an idle bot fully recovers (incl. teleport).
  • mission-progress (no flag) — only meaningful with a task, so gated on st.running: tool (hot-swap), stuck (stuck relative to a nav goal), hazard (feet in the void, lava or fire → RECOVER), hunger, human (yield the mission).

This is the complete reflex list (src/shared/reflexes/index.ts). Evaluation order is death → vitals → air → waterClutch → swimOut → tool → stuck → hazard → hunger → human.

This is deliberately not "run everything when idle" — only the five survival reflexes do. A broken tool on an idle bot does nothing; a drowning idle bot saves itself.

docs.title: Anti-false-positive: confirm before teleporting an idle bot
docs.text:
A survival divert to teleport-RECOVER must be confirmed, never a one-tick spike:

  • vitals distress requires repeated damage — ≥ cfg.safety.distressMinEvents distinct damage ticks within cfg.safety.distressWindow, not just "lost N HP". A single survived fall is one event → never trips (so an idle bot that took a fall but is now fine doesn't teleport for nothing); sustained drown / lava / suffocation racks up events → escapes.
  • The cfg.safety.minHealth floor fires immediately (you don't reach it from a glitch).
  • RECOVER mitigates in place first (surface via jump) and only teleports once on stable footing — a transient threat stabilises and never escalates.

docs.title: Below the reflexes: held keys while the worker tick blocks
docs.text:
Every reflex and every navigator veto runs inside a worker tick. A key that the bot holds stays held while a worker tick runs, so a tick that blocks lets the body walk with no check at all. In RCA I-4 a goto across a hollow-tower roof ran one synchronous extend-replan for about 25 s. Forward and sprint were still held from the previous step, and the bot walked off a 39-block rim. Two layers stop this:

  1. Release before a blocking replan. The executor releases the movement keys before each A* replan (releaseForBlockingWork in shared/nav/core.ts). The drive after the plan presses again what the new route wants. The airborne hold puts the released keys back, because it keeps the heading through a fall.
  2. Movement-key dead-man in main.js. main.js ticks on its own thread. When the worker heartbeat (mc_worker_alive) does not change for DEADMAN_STALE_TICKS (10) main ticks, main.js releases the movement, jump, sprint and sneak keys once for that stall. It also stops the forced sprint and writes a DEADMAN record to the journal, which get_logs shows. diag.main.deadman.stalls counts the stalls and lastStallTick gives the main tick of the last one. main.js cannot see which keys the worker held, so the count includes stalls with no key down; it is not a count of prevented falls. A worker that ticks normally changes the heartbeat every tick, so the dead-man does not act on it. When no worker runs (heartbeat 0), the dead-man does nothing, because a person can hold the keys. A stall also releases a key that a person holds at that time; the person must press it again.

The decision for layer 2 is deadmanStep (shared/harness/deadman.ts, with its plain-JS twin in harness/safe-io.js). test-ts/harness-contract.test.ts keeps the two equal.

The two layers stop the walk, not the stall. A long synchronous replan still blocks the worker for its whole length: on the I-4 roof one replan reads about a million cells, about 25 s live. During that time the keys are up and the bot stands still, and no reflex runs. A plan is not cut short by its read count. A cut turned a reachable leg behind a concave pocket (a lava lake, a wide ravine) into a false blocked_no_path; test-ts/nav-replan-safety.test.ts pins that such a leg arrives. The D* Lite engine (cfg.nav.dStar, off by default) searches across worker ticks, at most cfg.nav.dStarStepPops expansions per tick. The executor does not use it for a column leg (src/shared/nav/executor.ts), and the I-4 leg is a column leg, so its replan is one synchronous A* search.

docs.title: Prevention tier: one clutch-aware fall predicate
docs.text:
All "will this fall survive?" checks route through one SSOT predicate, canSurviveFall(drop, cap) (core/prim/movement-physics.ts):

canSurviveFall(drop, cap) = clutch  ∨  fallDamage(drop, waterBelow) ≤ maxFallDamage
  • The planner's cheap drop (dropDownSafe) passes clutch: false — a clutch dive is a separate, costed move (waterDrop), so the cheap drop must not silently offer fatal falls.
  • The executor's fall veto (src/shared/nav/executor.ts stepIsHazardous) passes clutch: true when a bucket is carried (the same gate the planner uses to offer a waterDrop). So the geofence can never veto a fall the water-clutch would save — planner and executor stay in lockstep, and the "with a bucket you can fall from any height" capability is honoured, not contradicted.

Note the recoverability guard (descent rim-veto, "can I climb back out?") is a different concern and is not clutch-aware — the clutch saves the fall, not the climb-back.

docs.title: Prevention tier: known-before-break digging
docs.text:
The drill's DESCEND shaft never breaks the floor under the bot unless it knows what is below. An unloaded or unsensed cell can hide a cave, lava or water, and breaking the floor over it drops the bot in. The rule does not cover EXCAVATE: its void guard (guardVoidCell, src/bot/missions/drill/excavate.ts) reads an unreadable cell as minecraft:stone.

  • The null convention. A senses BlockReader (src/shared/domain/senses.ts) returns null for an UNKNOWN cell. The drill reads its floor through knownReader (src/bot/missions/drill/descend.ts), which keeps an unreadable cell as null instead of masking it as stone.
  • The verdict. floorVerdict (src/bot/missions/drill/floor-safety.ts) returns unknown when the block to break, or any cell of the fall column down to the landing, reads null. floorUnsafe checks every support cell of the body's footprint (footprintAt).
  • The outcome. With no band mined yet, floorUnsafe logs DRILL_UNKNOWN_BELOW and calls skipUnreachableVein (src/bot/missions/drill/select-vein.ts): the bot goes to the next cached vein, or to PAUSED when none remains. It does not go to ERROR. With a band already mined, the unknown floor is the bottom of the shaft: DRILL_DEPTH_DONE, then PAUSED.

docs.title: Drowning: one hazard, three layers
docs.text:
Water is not a classifyBlock hazard, so drowning has its own predicate, submergesAt (src/shared/domain/senses.ts): feet cell AND head cell are water. Wading in 1-deep water stays allowed. Each layer sits in its own tier:

  1. Prevention — the navigator veto. stepIsHazardous (src/shared/nav/executor.ts) refuses a step when the step cell, or the landing below it, is submerging. The drill's own floorVerdict water verdict covers the shaft (see the rule above).
  2. Reaction — the swimOut reflex (src/shared/reflexes/swim-out.ts, survival: true). While the bot is submerged and breath is fine, swimOut holds jump and releases forward and sprint until the head clears water. It gives up after cfg.safety.swimOutMaxTicks ticks without a height gain. swimOut does not act in the settled phases RECOVER, PAUSED and ERROR (REFLEX_SETTLED, src/shared/kernel/phase.ts), so a bot that a drill skip left PAUSED in water has only the air reflex. The air reflex (src/shared/reflexes/air.ts) runs first and owns the terminal escape: when the breath fraction drops to cfg.safety.airRecoverPct, air diverts to RECOVER, which holds jump to surface before it teleports (src/bot/capabilities/recover.ts).
  3. Mark and skip — the drill's memory. recordDrowned (src/bot/missions/drill/floor-safety.ts) writes a drowned HazardMarker to mc_world.json through writeHazardMarker (src/shared/domain/world-model.ts). Two events write it: floorUnsafe on a water or void verdict with no band mined (DRILL_WATER, DRILL_VOID), and the DESCEND flooded-column watchdog after cfg.drill.waterContactTicks ticks of water contact with no band mined (DRILL_FLOODED_COLUMN). On the next run, selectDrillVein (src/bot/missions/drill/select-vein.ts) aims the vein at a column of its bounding box outside cfg.drill.hazardRadius of every marker, a peer's included. It drops the vein only when every candidate column is marked. The marker turns one abort into prevention for every later run.

docs.title: Client wedges are not a safety-tier concern
docs.text:
After a headless death the client process can stay without a loaded world while the bridge still answers. That is a process fault, not game state, so it is handled host-side by scripts/ops/wedge_watchdog.py (./gerda watchdog): detect, disconnect and reconnect, and optionally relaunch. It never touches the kernel or bundle. Needs a running bot:

./gerda watchdog --port 55545 --once                      # one check: exit 0 healthy, 3 wedged
./gerda watchdog --port 55545 --server localhost:25565    # watch; reconnect on a confirmed wedge

A relaunch of the instance happens only with --auto-relaunch <instance>; without it the watchdog prints the relaunch command and keeps watching.

docs.title: Scenario files: arenas, benches and sets
docs.text:
A scenario file is a JSON spec that builds a small scene in the live game and then tests or measures something in it. This page is the field reference for the three families the host tools read. How to run the gate and why it is shaped this way: TESTING.md. A tutorial for mod checks: MOD_TESTING.md.

Directory What it is Read by Shape scenarios/arenas/<name>.json Arena: build, then run a mission or a plan and assert its log events, or assert game state with checks scripts/dev/arena.py, scripts/dev/gate_live.py #/$defs/arena scenarios/bench/<name>.json Bench: build a course, then time navigator legs or one mission per planner scripts/dev/navbench.py, scripts/dev/gate_live.py #/$defs/bench scenarios/sets/<name>.json Film set: staging captured from the live world, no assertions scripts/dev/arena.py #/$defs/set

The shot lists in scenarios/shots/ are a different format, read by the shot runner: RIG.md § Shot runner.

The name of a spec is its file name without .json. An arena or set file that declares a name key does not load (scripts/dev/arena.py#_load).

docs.title: The schema and what checks it
docs.text:
scenarios/scenario.schema.json (JSON Schema 2020-12) states the shape of every family: the keys, their types, which are required, and which combinations are refused. The parsers read keys with plain dict access and ignore a key they do not know. Without the schema, a typo such as expcet would silently drop an arena out of the full gate.

scripts/tests/test_scenario_schema.py (part of just test-py, so of the pre-push just check) holds the schema in place:

  • every tracked file matches its $defs entry, and every arena and set also loads through scripts/dev/arena.py#_load, which adds the cross-field rules of scripts/dev/arena.py#validate_arena_spec and scripts/dev/arena.py#validate_set_spec;
  • every key the three parsers read is in the schema, and every schema key is read by a parser;
  • every key and op kind in the schema is named on this page, and the examples on this page validate;
  • every event in expect.events and every done_event is a string literal in src/, every mission name has a ### heading in MISSIONS.md, and every plan name is a plan in src/bot/plans/.

To check a new file before you run it in the game:

python3 -m unittest discover -s scripts/tests -t scripts/tests -p test_scenario_schema.py

docs.title: A minimal arena
docs.text:
{
  "desc": "goto walks 8 blocks over flat stone; PASS = GOTO_ARRIVED, no ERROR",
  "ops": [
    { "op": "clear", "from": [-2, 101, -2], "to": [10, 104, 2] },
    { "op": "fill", "from": [-2, 100, -2], "to": [10, 100, 2], "block": "minecraft:stone" },
    { "op": "clearinv" },
    { "op": "give", "item": "minecraft:diamond_pickaxe" },
    { "op": "select", "slot": 0 },
    { "op": "player", "pos": [0, 101, 0] }
  ],
  "mission": { "name": "goto", "params": { "x": 8, "y": 101, "z": 0 } },
  "expect": { "events": ["GOTO_ARRIVED"], "timeout": 60 }
}

scenarios/arenas/goto-travel.json is this arena.

docs.title: Arena keys
docs.text:
Key Type Required / default Meaning Parser desc string optional One line printed by build and list. Say what PASS proves. scripts/dev/arena.py#build ops list of ops required, at least one Build the scene and kit the bot, in order. scripts/dev/arena.py#_build_ops mission object optional The mission to start after the build: name (a mission in MISSIONS.md) and params (an object, default {}, the mission's parameters as documented there). Sent as mission_start. scripts/dev/arena.py#run plan string optional; not with mission A plan name from src/bot/plans/ (for example sustain-cycle), sent as plan_start. The orchestrator chains its steps. scripts/dev/arena.py#run marker object optional; needs mission or plan A prospector vein for the drill mission: ore (an ore intent, such as iron), x, z (integers). Written into the world store after the worker restart and before the mission starts. scripts/dev/arena.py#_seed_marker expect object optional; needs mission or plan The log events that prove the mission worked: the expect block. scripts/dev/arena.py#run checks list of checks optional, at least one jeval assertions on game state. scripts/dev/arena.py#run_checks known_bad string optional Marks the arena as a negative control and says which wrong behaviour it asserts: known-bad arenas. scripts/dev/arena.py#validate_arena_spec

What run does, in order (scripts/dev/arena.py#run): build the ops; with neither mission nor plan, run the checks and stop (no checks: build only, a PASS). Otherwise restart the worker, respawn the bot if it is dead and teleport it back to the first player op (scripts/dev/arena.py#_ensure_bot_ready), seed marker, start the mission or plan, wait for expect, then run the checks.

Gate membership. just gate-live with no names runs every arena that asserts something: a non-empty expect.events, or checks (scripts/dev/arena.py#asserts). An arena with neither, such as parkour-gap2, is a build-only fixture you run by name. The --quick core is the list CORE in scripts/dev/gate_live.py.

docs.title: The expect block
docs.text:
Key Type Required / default Meaning events list of strings required, at least one Event names from the bot's log, such as ORE_FOUND, GOTO_ARRIVED, DRILL_VEIN_REACHED. Every one must appear. Order and count do not matter. timeout number (seconds) default 60 Wall-clock time to wait for all of them.

The runner polls the log once a second and reads only the entries after the last BOOT, so an earlier worker boot cannot pass or fail this run (scripts/dev/arena.py#_recent_events). The arena FAILS when an event is still missing at the timeout, or when any TRANSITION to ERROR was logged, even if every event arrived. Name events the mission emits on every run, not ones that depend on remembered world state: TESTING.md § Adding an arena.

With a mission but no expect, run runs the checks right after the mission starts, without waiting for the mission.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
A check runs one jeval (the privileged bridge command: full jsMacros and Java scope, including srg(class, member) from harness/ext.js) and compares the value of its last expression with expect.

Key Type Required / default Meaning Parser desc string optional; default: the first 60 characters of jeval Printed on the PASS/FAIL line. scripts/dev/arena.py#check_outcome jeval string, not blank required JavaScript. Wrap several statements in an IIFE, (function () { …; return v; })(). scripts/dev/arena.py#validate_arena_spec expect any JSON value required The exact value jeval must return. scripts/dev/arena.py#check_outcome wrong true optional; only in a known_bad arena This check's expect is wrong on purpose. scripts/dev/arena.py#wrong_outcome

expect is compared as canonical JSON (json.dumps(…, sort_keys=True), scripts/dev/arena.py#_canon): true is not 1, 1 is not 1.0, and the key order of an object does not matter. An object must match whole. With "expect": { "held": "minecraft:iron_pickaxe", "drops": true }, the jeval has to return an object with exactly those two keys and values; a missing key, an extra key or "drops": 1 is a FAIL. A jeval error is a FAIL that prints the error. Every check runs, also after one fails, and the list passes only when all of them pass.

{
  "desc": "an iron pickaxe harvests tungstate ore",
  "ops": [
    { "op": "clear", "from": [-2, 101, -2], "to": [2, 104, 3] },
    { "op": "fill", "from": [-2, 100, -2], "to": [2, 100, 3], "block": "minecraft:stone" },
    { "op": "set", "pos": [0, 101, 2], "block": "gtceu:tungstate_ore" },
    { "op": "clearinv" },
    { "op": "give", "item": "minecraft:iron_pickaxe" },
    { "op": "player", "pos": [0, 101, 0] },
    { "op": "wait", "ticks": 40 }
  ],
  "checks": [
    {
      "desc": "the placed block is GTCEu tungstate ore",
      "jeval": "World.getBlock(0, 101, 2).getId()",
      "expect": "gtceu:tungstate_ore"
    },
    {
      "desc": "an iron pickaxe in hand gets the drop",
      "jeval": "(function () { Player.openInventory().setSelectedHotbarSlotIndex(0); var p = Player.getPlayer(); var state = World.getBlock(0, 101, 2).getBlockStateHelper().getRaw(); return { held: p.getMainHand().getItemId(), drops: p.getRaw()[srg('Player', 'hasCorrectToolForDrops')](state) }; })()",
      "expect": { "held": "minecraft:iron_pickaxe", "drops": true }
    }
  ]
}

The full pair is scenarios/arenas/gtceu-ore-harvest-tier.json and its known-bad twin.

docs.title: Known-bad arenas
docs.text:
A known-bad arena proves that a check can fail. The rules, all enforced at load (scripts/dev/arena.py#validate_arena_spec):

  • known_bad is a non-blank string, and the arena marks at least one check "wrong": true. A wrong check outside a known_bad arena is refused, and so is any wrong value but true.
  • Each wrong check has exactly one unmarked twin in the same arena: the same jeval text and a different expect, the right value (scripts/dev/arena.py#twin_index).

A wrong check PASSES only when its jeval succeeded, returned exactly its twin's expect, and the twin passed (scripts/dev/arena.py#wrong_outcome). The wrong value itself, a null, a third value or an error is a FAIL. No verdict is inverted. Why and how to write one: MOD_TESTING.md.

docs.title: Ops
docs.text:
Every op is an object with an op key. Coordinates are lists of three integers [x, y, z]; boxes are inclusive and their corners can come in any order. Build ops go to the game as chat commands, so the driven client must be opped. Each op is one bridge round-trip (scripts/dev/arena.py#_apply_op).

op Other keys Effect clear from, to /fill … minecraft:air over the box. fill from, to, block /fill the box with block. block goes into the command as written, so it can carry a block state or NBT (minecraft:chest{Items:[…]}). Vanilla /fill refuses a box of more than 32768 blocks. set pos, block /setblock one block. clearinv — /clear @s: empty the bot's inventory. give item, count (integer ≥ 1, default 1) /give @s. select slot (integer 0–8) Select a hotbar slot (taps key.hotbar.<slot + 1>). player pos /tp @s to the centre of the block: x + 0.5, y, z + 0.5. An arena's first player op is also its start, where the bot is put back before the mission. marker ore, x, z Write a prospector vein into the world store at once, host-side. wait ticks (integer ≥ 0) Sleep ticks / 20 seconds on the host, for example to let the server sync blocks and items to the client before the checks read them.

clean sets every clear, fill and set region back to air (scripts/dev/arena.py#clean). Build and clean hold a /forceload ticket on the touched chunks while they write (scripts/dev/arena.py#forceload_box). Arenas build at fixed coordinates, and each clean clears only its own regions, so two arenas must not overlap.

A marker op and a top-level marker write the world store of the instance in MC_INST (default: the human instance; gate_live.py --port points it at that bot's instance).

docs.title: Benches
docs.text:
A bench races navigator legs, or one whole mission, per planner. Running and reading the results: navbench.md.

{
  "desc": "flat sprint, 12 blocks",
  "ops": [
    { "op": "clear", "from": [39, 88, -1], "to": [70, 94, 3] },
    { "op": "fill", "from": [39, 88, -1], "to": [70, 88, 3], "block": "minecraft:stone" },
    { "op": "clearinv" }
  ],
  "start": [41, 89, 1],
  "legs": [{ "name": "flat12", "to": [53, 89, 1] }],
  "repeats": 3,
  "timeout": 25
}
Key Type Required / default Meaning Parser name string default: the file name The label of the report. scripts/dev/navbench.py#_load desc string optional Printed by build. scripts/dev/navbench.py#build ops list of ops optional The same op vocabulary, without player: the runner teleports the bot to start itself before every run. scripts/dev/navbench.py#build start [x, y, z] required Where every run starts. scripts/dev/navbench.py#_anchor legs list of { "name", "to" } a leg bench: required; not with mission Each leg drives from start to to through the nav probe. scripts/dev/navbench.py#run mission { "name", "params" } a mission bench: required; not with legs One whole mission per run, timed from mission_start to done_event. scripts/dev/navbench.py#race_mission marker { "ore", "x", "z" } optional; needs mission A vein seeded after each worker restart, for drill. scripts/dev/navbench.py#race_mission collect item id optional; needs mission The item whose bag count before and after the run is the yield. scripts/dev/navbench.py#race_mission done_event string default SCAN_EXHAUSTED; needs mission The event that ends a mission run (drill ends at VEINS_DEPLETED). scripts/dev/navbench.py#race_mission impls list of astar, dstar default ["astar"] The planners to race. greedy is an alias of astar; any other name stops the run. scripts/dev/navbench.py#_engine repeats integer ≥ 1 default 3 (legs), 2 (mission) Runs per leg and planner. scripts/dev/navbench.py#run, scripts/dev/navbench.py#run_mission timeout number (seconds) default 30 (legs), 220 (mission) Per run. scripts/dev/navbench.py#run, scripts/dev/navbench.py#run_mission arrival number or null default (null, 0): cfg.nav.gotoArrivalDist How close to to counts as arrived, in blocks. scripts/dev/navbench.py#race_leg

just gate-live runs every bench with legs and no mission, A* only, each leg once with one retry; PASS = arrived on every leg (scripts/dev/gate_live.py#_gate_bench).

docs.title: Film sets
docs.text:
A set is staging for a filmed scene: the arena format without assertions, plus a snapshot declaration. run --all and just gate-live never read scenarios/sets/; a set is addressed as sets/<name>. Workflow: RIG.md § Sets.

{
  "desc": "a 3x3 pad",
  "snapshot": {
    "boxes": [{ "from": [0, 100, 0], "to": [2, 101, 2] }],
    "dimension": "minecraft:overworld"
  },
  "ops_generated": [
    { "op": "clear", "from": [0, 100, 0], "to": [2, 101, 2] },
    { "op": "fill", "from": [0, 100, 0], "to": [2, 100, 2], "block": "minecraft:stone" }
  ],
  "ops": [{ "op": "marker", "ore": "iron", "x": 1, "z": 1 }]
}
Key Type Required / default Meaning Parser desc string optional As for an arena. scripts/dev/arena.py#build snapshot object required boxes: a non-empty list of { "from", "to" } boxes to capture, each at most 32768 cells (SNAPSHOT_MAX_CELLS). dimension: a namespaced dimension id, stamped by snapshot; build and clean refuse a client in another dimension. scripts/dev/arena.py#validate_set_spec, scripts/dev/arena.py#_assert_dimension ops_generated list of clear/fill/set ops written by snapshot A generated file section: re-run snapshot, never edit it by hand. scripts/dev/arena.py#compress_box ops list of ops optional Hand-written setup applied after ops_generated: marker, give, player, select, wait, and any block a snapshot cannot express (stairs and slabs restage in their default orientation). scripts/dev/arena.py#_build_ops

A set that declares mission, plan, expect, checks or known_bad does not load. A build over 2000 ops is refused (BUILD_MAX_OPS, scripts/dev/arena.py#_check_op_budget).

docs.title: Running a scenario
docs.text:
just gate-live mine-vein drill-vein                    # named arenas through the gate (no benches)
just gate-live                                         # every asserting arena + every leg bench
python3 scripts/dev/arena.py list                      # arenas and sets, with their desc
python3 scripts/dev/arena.py run mine-vein --port <p>  # one arena: build, run, verify; exit 0/1
python3 scripts/dev/arena.py build mine-vein           # only build the scene
python3 scripts/dev/arena.py clean mine-vein           # its regions back to air
./gerda bench run flat                                 # one bench

arena.py run does not clean up after itself; gate_live.py cleans each arena, pass or fail. Run every live scenario against an opped test bot in a flat test area, and confirm the connected player is the bot: TESTING.md § Layer 3.

docs.title: Dedicated server setup (multi-bot fleet)
docs.text: Runbook for the Monifactory dedicated server the bot fleet connects to. Verified on Monifactory 0.13.4 (MC 1.20.1 / Forge 47.4.13) with 4 bots in one shared world.

docs.title: Why dedicated, not "Open to LAN"
docs.text: LAN-open ties the world to a host client, pauses it when the host opens a menu, picks a random port each time, and its discovery is unreliable between instances on one host. A dedicated server runs 24/7 and is what the fleet coordinator hub (FLEET_PLAYBOOK § 2) expects. The bots run inside jsMacros (a client mod), so they are ordinary clients; the server is plain Forge plus the Monifactory server mods.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Java 17+ (Java 21 works for Forge 47.x — verified). The server needs a system Java — the launcher's own Java only serves the clients. Ubuntu/Debian, with the download tools §1 uses: sudo apt install openjdk-17-jre-headless curl unzip.
  • Disk: ~2 GB for the server + world.
  • The matching client instances already installed (Prism/MultiMC/FreesmLauncher — adjust to your launcher), one per bot.

docs.title: 1. Get the official server pack
docs.text:
Monifactory is not on Modrinth, and the CurseForge API needs a key — but the author ships server zips on GitHub: Omicron-Industries/Monifactory → Releases (formerly ThePansmith/Monifactory). Download the Monifactory-Beta.<version>-server.zip matching your client version (here 0.13.4).

# Run from the repo root. Installs into <serverRoot>/monifactory-0.13.4; serverRoot defaults
# to ~/mc-servers. To change it, set "serverRoot" in local.config.json or export MC_SERVER_ROOT.
SRV="$(python3 scripts/local_config.py server_dir)"
mkdir -p "$SRV" && cd "$SRV"
curl -sL -o server.zip \
  https://github.com/Omicron-Industries/Monifactory/releases/download/0.13.4/Monifactory-Beta.0.13.4-server.zip
unzip -q server.zip && rm server.zip   # → config/ mods/ kubejs/ defaultconfigs/ manifest.json

The zip is overrides only (mods + configs) — no Forge, no MC jar. Install those next.

Leave config-overrides/ (the pack's normal / hardmode / expert modes) alone: the bot is tuned on the default mode. If you switch modes, switch the server and every client the same way.

docs.title: 2. Install the Forge server
docs.text:
cd "$SRV"
curl -sL -o forge-installer.jar \
  https://maven.minecraftforge.net/net/minecraftforge/forge/1.20.1-47.4.13/forge-1.20.1-47.4.13-installer.jar
java -jar forge-installer.jar --installServer   # writes run.sh, libraries/, user_jvm_args.txt

docs.title: 3. Two required fixes (the 0.13.4 server pack does not boot as-is)
3a. monilabs crashes the dedicated server → bump it
docs.text:
The 0.13.4 server pack ships monilabs 0.21.2, which loads a client-only render class (PrismFX$PositionalColor) during common_setup and dies with Attempted to load class … for invalid dist DEDICATED_SERVER. Fix: replace it with a later build from NegaNote/MoniLabs releases (0.21.7 verified; identical deps — forge[47,) / mc[1.20.1,) / gtceu[7.5.2,), all satisfied by the pack). This is the same monilabs the pack itself ships in 0.13.5/0.13.6.

cd "$SRV/mods"
rm -f monilabs-0.21.2.jar
curl -sLO https://github.com/NegaNote/MoniLabs/releases/download/1.20.1-0.21.7/monilabs-0.21.7.jar

Apply the same monilabs version to every CLIENT instance too (mods/ folder) — Forge's mod-version handshake + registry sync must match between client and server, or the client is rejected on connect.

docs.title: 3b. Parallel mod-loading deadlock → single-thread it
docs.text:
The pack intermittently deadlocks during boot (a class-loading race between KubeJS plugin loading, alltheleaks, and MixinSquared on the parallel modloading-worker pool — the log freezes and jstack <pid> shows "Found one Java-level deadlock" in MixinLaunchPluginLegacy.handlesClass). Force single-threaded mod loading.

The pack ships no config/fml.toml, and Forge writes one only on the first start — the start that can deadlock. Create it before the first start, with only these two keys; Forge fills in the rest:

cd "$SRV"
printf 'maxThreads = 1\nversionCheck = false\n' > config/fml.toml

maxThreads = 1 (Forge's default is -1) is what Forge's ModWorkManager reads (FMLConfig.MAX_THREADS). versionCheck = false is optional; it silences the version-check network threads.

Boot then takes ~2 min of mod load + world-gen and reaches Done (…).

Debugging tip for any "modded server boot hangs with no log output": jstack <pid> — if the main thread is parked in ModLoader.waitForTransition and there's a deadlock cycle, it's a parallel-load race; maxThreads = 1 resolves it.

docs.title: 4. Configure + run
docs.text:
cd "$SRV"
echo 'eula=true' > eula.txt
# user_jvm_args.txt: heap (GT server is heavy) — e.g.
printf -- '-Xms4G\n-Xmx8G\n' >> user_jvm_args.txt

Key server.properties for the fleet (loopback/LAN only — offline-mode has no auth). The server writes this file on its first start. Either create it now with only these lines (the server adds the other keys), or start once, stop, and edit it. A .properties file has no inline comments — a # after a value becomes part of the value, and the server then silently falls back to the default — so each comment sits on its own line:

# bots use fixed offline usernames: no MS auth, sessions never expire
online-mode=false
server-port=25565
# bots mine and build at spawn
spawn-protection=0
# bots do not melee-damage each other when hunting
pvp=false
# passive animals still spawn (hunt works); no hostiles, no hunger. Raise it when wanted
difficulty=peaceful
max-players=10
# offline accounts have no signed chat profile to check
enforce-secure-profile=false

Back in the repo root, install the control wrapper (§ server-ctl.sh below) and start the server:

cp scripts/ops/server-ctl.sh "$SRV/"
"$SRV/server-ctl.sh" start
"$SRV/server-ctl.sh" log               # repeat until `Done (…)! For help`

Check that the port is open with ss -ltn | grep 25565.

On first boot, turn off the day/night cycle so the world stays in daylight (the fleet plays always-day, see FLEET_PLAYBOOK § 1). The setting is saved with the world:

"$SRV/server-ctl.sh" cmd "time set day"
"$SRV/server-ctl.sh" cmd "gamerule doDaylightCycle false"

Set the FTB Essentials /home cooldown to 0. The bots teleport home to recover from water, lava and the void, and FTB Essentials refuses a /home sent within the cooldown (default 10 s) of the previous one: the bot stays put, which it cannot tell from a missing home. The setting is home.cooldown in world/serverconfig/ftbessentials.snbt (relative to $SRV); the fleet server uses cooldown: 0. Restart the server after the change. With a cooldown left on, the bot gives up on /home after cfg.safety.homeNoEffectLimit refused recoveries and tries again cfg.safety.homeRearmTicks later.

docs.title: 5. Connect the bots
docs.text:
Per-bot instance creation and resource tuning (heap + render floor so 4+ clients fit on one host) is its own runbook: BOT_INSTANCE_SETUP.md.

  1. Create each bot instance as in BOT_INSTANCE_SETUP § 1. That section is the one place that states the naming contract (instance names, offline accounts, bridge ports) and how each client connects to 127.0.0.1:25565.
  2. Leave the bots non-op. Each bot plays like a real player; its only privilege is FTB Essentials teleport — the commands are listed in FLEET_PLAYBOOK § 1. A test bot is opped for one just gate-live session (op <name>, de-op after), because arenas build blocks.
  3. Check each bridge: ./gerda ctl --bot <instance> ping → pong.

docs.title: server-ctl.sh (detached run + FIFO console)
docs.text:
A small control wrapper so the server runs in the background and console commands (op, list, stop) can be sent from any shell. It ships as scripts/ops/server-ctl.sh; copy it into $SRV (§ 4) — it works on the directory it sits in, and scripts/local_config.py server_ctl looks for it there.

"$SRV/server-ctl.sh" start            # detached; console output goes to $SRV/console.log
"$SRV/server-ctl.sh" cmd "op bot_1"   # any console command
"$SRV/server-ctl.sh" status
"$SRV/server-ctl.sh" log              # last 40 lines of logs/latest.log
"$SRV/server-ctl.sh" stop             # waits for the world save (up to 120 s), then returns

Wait for stop to return before you start the server again. The server reads its console from a FIFO whose write end a sleep process holds open; do not kill that process while the server runs — end of input on the console stops the server without a line in the log.

The server files live outside this repo ($SRV = python3 scripts/local_config.py server_dir) and are not committed; this runbook is how to reproduce them.

docs.title: Setup — from zero to a driven bot
docs.text:
For anyone running the bot in a real game for the first time. Follow the Quickstart in order: it starts on a machine with nothing installed and ends with a bot that answers over the bridge. Steps 1–2 need no game; steps 3–4 install it; step 5 deploys into it; steps 6–7 need it running. For more than one bot, do this once, then see SERVER_SETUP.md and BOT_INSTANCE_SETUP.md.

What you end up with: a Minecraft 1.20.1 Forge instance of the Monifactory modpack with the jsMacros mod, and this repo deploying the bot into it. The bot's GTCEu intelligence (prospector, ore registry, quest tooling) is tuned to that pack. Budget about 8 GB of RAM for one game client.

Another Minecraft version, or no modpack? The harness (bridge, ./gerda ctl, MCP, screenshots) runs on every version that has a jsMacros build, Forge or Fabric; Gerda Bot's movement needs Forge. PORTABILITY.md has the tested support matrix and a short recipe for a plain vanilla + jsMacros instance — follow it instead of step 3 below.

docs.title: 1. Get the code
docs.text:
You need git, curl, unzip and Python 3.11 or newer. Ubuntu/Debian:

sudo apt install git curl unzip python3

Fedora: sudo dnf install git curl unzip python3. macOS: xcode-select --install gives git; curl and unzip are preinstalled. Windows: winget install --id=Git.Git (Git Bash comes with it).

Clone the repo and enter it — every command below runs from its root:

git clone https://github.com/flamerix-ai/gerda.git
cd gerda

Clone it; do not download the ZIP. The commit gates (just hooks) and several tools need the .git directory.

docs.title: 2. Install the tools
docs.text:
Have Nix on x86_64 Linux? Then this step is one command. The repo's flake.nix pins every tool below:

nix develop      # or, with nix-direnv: `direnv allow` once — the shell then loads on every cd

The default shell carries bun, Node 22, Python 3.12, just, ffmpeg with ffprobe, fd and entr (for just watch), git, and Vineflower with JDK 21 (for ./gerda decompile). The filming rig has its own shell, nix develop .#capture (headless sway, wf-recorder, grim) — see RIG.md. The flake does not carry uv, which only the MCP server needs: nix shell nixpkgs#uv. Then skip to bun install and just hooks below — those two are still yours to run. The flake declares x86_64-linux only; on macOS or ARM, use the installers.

Without Nix: bun builds the bot, just runs the recipes, ffmpeg (with its ffprobe) is needed by just check, whose python suites run real clips, and uv runs the MCP server (optional — only for LLM operators).

# Linux / macOS
curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash        # bun
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh # uv (optional, for the MCP server)
sudo apt install just ffmpeg                    # Ubuntu 24.04+; dnf / pacman -S / brew install just ffmpeg

Both installers add their directory to PATH through your shell profile: open a new terminal before you go on.

# Windows (PowerShell)
powershell -c "irm bun.sh/install.ps1 | iex"    # bun
winget install --id=astral-sh.uv                # uv (optional)
winget install --id=Python.Python.3.12         # python
winget install --id=Casey.Just                  # just
winget install --id=Gyan.FFmpeg                 # ffmpeg + ffprobe

winget and the bun installer add their directories to PATH for new terminals only (Path environment variable modified; restart your shell), so open a new Git Bash before you go on.

On Windows, run the commands of this guide in Git Bash (it came with Git in step 1): just runs its recipes through Git's bash, which it finds through the PATH of Git Bash; from cmd or PowerShell it stops with "could not find the shell env", unless Git's usr\bin is on the system PATH. With WSL installed, a bare bash typed in cmd or PowerShell is WSL's bash.exe, not Git's. Two names differ in Git Bash:

  • python, not python3. The Python installer provides python and py; python3 starts the Microsoft Store stub (Python was not found, exit 49). The just recipes pick python on their own.
  • python gerda <cmd>, not ./gerda <cmd>: the script's first line asks for python3. From cmd or PowerShell, gerda.cmd <cmd> works too, but the JSON of ctl send needs other quoting there than in the examples below.

The Python host-tool suites assume Linux or macOS, so just check and the pre-push hook fail on Windows. Run just check-ts, the TypeScript half that the pre-commit hook runs, and contribute from WSL.

Then install the TypeScript toolchain and point git at the repo's gates:

bun install     # the TS toolchain, into node_modules/
just hooks      # the versioned git hooks (no CI — they ARE the gate; stages: docs/TESTING.md)

Optional extras:

  • just watch (rebuild + redeploy on every save) needs fd and entr. Ubuntu names the fd binary fdfind: sudo apt install fd-find entr, then mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && ln -s "$(command -v fdfind)" ~/.local/bin/fd.
  • ./gerda decompile needs vineflower and a JDK; ./gerda capture and ./gerda parkour --video need the Nix capture shell (Wayland tools). Each one's -h says what it needs.

docs.title: 3. Get the game
docs.text:
A launcher keeps each modpack in its own instance: a folder instances/<name>/ with its own mods, configs and worlds; the game files live in instances/<name>/minecraft/. The bot deploys into that minecraft/ folder.

  1. Install a MultiMC-format launcher. FreesmLauncher (supports offline accounts; on Linux the portable tarball or the AppImage, on Windows the FreesmLauncher-Windows-MSVC-Setup-<version>.exe installer, -MSVC-arm64-Setup- on ARM) or Prism Launcher (offline accounts need one Microsoft login first). The launcher downloads the Java the game needs; you do not install Java for the client. (A dedicated server needs a system Java — SERVER_SETUP.md.)
  2. Add an account. Accounts → Add Offline → a name such as bot_1. If the launcher's first-run wizard offers to fetch the official launcher's key, skip it; this pack does not need it.
  3. Import the Monifactory 0.13.4 client. Add Instance → Import → paste https://github.com/Omicron-Industries/Monifactory/releases/download/0.13.4/Monifactory-Beta.0.13.4-client.zip and name the instance Monifactory — the tools assume that name for your own instance (BOT_INSTANCE_SETUP § 1 has the naming rules). Accept the optional-mods dialog. The launcher then downloads about 220 mods; this takes a few minutes. Keep the client on 0.13.4: a dedicated server must run the same version. Joining the dedicated server? Swap monilabs on this client too (SERVER_SETUP §3a).
  4. Tell the repo where the instances are. just sync autodetects the launcher's instances/ dir only for installed launchers (~/.local/share/{FreesmLauncher,PrismLauncher,MultiMC}, the Prism flatpak, and the macOS/Windows equivalents). A portable launcher (the FreesmLauncher tarball, MultiMC) keeps instances/ next to its own binary, and autodetect misses it. The launcher opens that folder from its toolbar: Folders → Instances. Set it once:
cp local.config.json.example local.config.json
# edit local.config.json: "instancesRoot": "~/apps/FreesmLauncher/instances"
# (or: export MC_INSTANCES_ROOT=~/apps/FreesmLauncher/instances)

For one bot, instancesRoot is the only key you need; the account keys in the example are for the multi-bot and filming tools, which ask for them when they run.

docs.title: 4. Install jsMacros
docs.text:
The bot runs inside the jsMacros mod. Download ONE file — jsMacros 1.9.2 for Forge 1.20.1 — into the instance's mods/ folder:

MODS="$(python3 scripts/local_config.py instance_dir Monifactory)/minecraft/mods"
curl -L -o "$MODS/jsmacros-1.20.1-1.9.2-forge.jar" \
  https://cdn.modrinth.com/data/3wGWhm8A/versions/7kPvvJff/jsmacros-1.20.1-1.9.2-forge.jar

(The same file is on Modrinth — Forge, 1.20.1 — and in the jsMacros GitHub releases.) The jar already contains the JavaScript language (GraalJS, ES2022 — what the bundle targets) and unpacks it into config/jsMacros/LanguageExtensions/ on the first start; there is no separate extension to install.

Start the instance from the launcher, wait for the title screen, and quit (Quit Game). Then do it once more. The first start creates minecraft/config/jsMacros/Macros/ — just sync deploys into it — and a config/jsMacros/options.json with "version": 2; the second start migrates that file to "version": 3 and empties its service list. Services registered before that migration are lost, so step 6 waits for version 3. A Config Failed To Load line in the first log is harmless.

docs.title: 5. Build and deploy
docs.text:
just check      # tsc + biome + defensive-checker + vitest + python suites — offline, no game needed
just build      # tsup → dist/__gerda_bot.bundle.js
just sync       # build + copy the bundle and the service harness into the instance

just sync writes the bundle plus the services (bridge.js, main.js, worker.js, ext.js, shared modules) into <instance>/minecraft/config/jsMacros/Macros/ of every instance that has that folder, and gives each a distinct bridge port (bridge_port.txt; registry in the gitignored mc-bots.json, which keeps existing ports across syncs). How instances are named and how ports are handed out: BOT_INSTANCE_SETUP.md § 1. If it says No deploy targets, go back to step 4: the game has not been started with jsMacros yet. Rewriting the service files under a running client restarts its jsMacros services, so while another client is running, keep it out with just sync --skip <thatInstance> (repeatable).

Generate the SRG name map (once per Minecraft version). Forge keeps obfuscated SRG names for class members (m_7583_). The harness resolves them through harness/srg_names.json, a generated file that is not in the repo. Build it from the mappings your launcher downloaded when you started the instance in step 4, then deploy it:

./gerda srg --build                           # index the on-disk mappings
./gerda srg --export harness/srg_names.json   # write the SRG → Mojang map
just sync                                     # ship it next to the services

This enables the srg() helper in jeval, the Mojang names in reflect, and the boot self-check of every hardcoded SRG name (diag reports it as srgCheck). Without the file the bot still runs, but the self-check is skipped and srgCheck reads unknown. Regenerate it after a Minecraft or Forge version change.

docs.title: 6. Register the services (in-game, once)
docs.text:
bridge.js and main.js are jsMacros Service scripts; register each once. Do not register worker.js: main.js registers and starts it itself. First check that <instance>/minecraft/config/jsMacros/options.json says "version": 3 — if it says 2, start the game once more and quit (step 4).

In the game (GUI). Start the game and enter a world (single-player, or your server).

  1. Open the jsMacros GUI: Esc → Mods → search JS (the mod is listed as "JS Macros"; searching jsmacros finds nothing) → JS Macros → Config. jsMacros' default key J does not work in Monifactory — JourneyMap takes it. For a hotkey, rebind "JS Macros GUI" under Options → Controls → Key Binds.
  2. Open the Services tab.
  3. Click +, type main, Confirm. In the new row, click the file cell (./), pick main.js, Select. Click Disabled so it reads Enabled, and Stopped so it reads Running.
  4. The same for bridge: + → bridge → Confirm → file bridge.js → Enabled → Running. The file picker truncates names: bridge.js and bridge_port.txt both show as bridge…; bridge.js is the first.
  5. Leave with Esc, and end the session with Quit Game: jsMacros saves the list on a clean quit, and a crash loses changes made in that session.

Without the GUI (config file). With the game closed, add both services to core.services in options.json. The file path is relative to config/jsMacros/Macros/:

"services": {
  "main":   {"file": "main.js",   "enabled": true},
  "bridge": {"file": "bridge.js", "enabled": true}
}

Or let a script make that edit (game closed, file at version 3):

OPTS="$(python3 scripts/local_config.py instance_dir Monifactory)/minecraft/config/jsMacros/options.json"
python3 -c 'import json,sys; p=sys.argv[1]; o=json.load(open(p)); assert o["version"]==3, "start the game once more first"; o["core"]["services"].update({"main":{"file":"main.js","enabled":True},"bridge":{"file":"bridge.js","enabled":True}}); json.dump(o,open(p,"w"),indent=2)' "$OPTS"

Edit the file only while the game is closed: a running game keeps the list in memory and writes it back over the file. On the next start the services start by themselves, before you join a world.

From then on everything reloads headlessly (reload_main, reload_ext, reload_worker bridge commands) — you never need the GUI again.

docs.title: 7. Check it works
docs.text:
./gerda ctl ping        # → pong (bridge reachable)
./gerda ctl status      # services + worker heartbeat
./gerda ctl get_state   # position, health, held tool, worker status
./gerda ctl send mission_start '{"name": "goto", "params": {"x": 100, "y": 64, "z": 200}}'   # the navigator walks there

For goto, pick a point about 20 blocks from the pos that get_state printed: a far target in unexplored terrain takes long to reach. In single-player the game pauses while its window does not have focus, and the bot stops with it. To keep it running while you type in the terminal, press F3+P in the game once, or set pauseOnLostFocus:false in the instance's options.txt with the game closed.

With no bridge, ctl prints one ERR: no bridge at <host>:<port> … line saying what to check (the game running, in a world, with main and bridge enabled). If the bot bundle did not load, every bot command answers no module loaded, ctl status exits 1 with an ERR: worker load_failed: … line, and get_state has the detail under worker.fatal.

./gerda is the repo-root CLI fronting every host tool; ./gerda ctl is sugar for python3 scripts/ops/bridge_ctl.py. Run ./gerda bare for the full list, and ./gerda <cmd> -h for any tool's help. None of this starts the autonomous loop; the goto mission walks only to the point you give it (MISSIONS.md § goto). Note that ./gerda ctl goto x y z is something else: a Baritone #goto chat command, which without Baritone only posts #goto … in chat — on a server, for everyone to read.

docs.title: Wire the MCP server (optional, for LLM operators)
docs.text:
cp .mcp.json.example .mcp.json    # gitignored; adjust port if not 55544

Claude Code started in the repo root reads that file. For any other MCP client, register the stdio command uv run mcp/server.py in that client, with the same environment variables. Either way the client gets the mc_* tools: mc_ping, mc_get_state, and the generic mc_send(type, args) for every bridge command — discover the full set via the mc://api resource. On a single machine, set MC_BRIDGE_HOST to 127.0.0.1; auto also tries the WSL gateway. Details, environment variables, and the fleet tools: mcp/README.md. The server reads its config once at startup — reconnect it after changing .mcp.json.

docs.title: Push metrics (optional)
docs.text:
Telemetry is off by default. The bot can push its counters and gauges (blocks mined, phase, health, deaths, …) as Prometheus text to a VictoriaMetrics import endpoint. To turn it on, put the URL in the gitignored config/local.overrides.json, then just sync and ./gerda reload-worker:

{"telemetry": {"pushUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:8428/api/v1/import/prometheus"}}

Metric names start with miner_ (cfg.telemetry.prefix); a push goes out every cfg.telemetry.interval ticks. If the endpoint is down, the journal gets one TELEMETRY_PUSH_FAIL per outage and a TELEMETRY_PUSH_RECOVERED when pushes work again.

docs.title: Run a mission
docs.text:
First, once, give the bot a home on a safe spot. Its recovery and low-health retreat teleport there with /home base:

./gerda ctl send chat '{"message": "/sethome base"}'

Then a mission a fresh bot can do with an empty bag:

./gerda ctl send mission_start '{"name": "chop", "params": {"count": 4}}'
./gerda ctl send mission_status
./gerda ctl pause     # hand control back
./gerda ctl resume

chop finds trees near the bot, walks to them and fells them; it stops after 4 logs, or sooner if it finds no more. Without an axe it logs MISSION_TOOL_MISSING and breaks the logs by hand, slowly. Trees inside spawn protection can't be cut: the server refuses a non-op player's break within the spawn-protection radius of server.properties (16 blocks by default) and inside claimed chunks. Walk or teleport a few dozen blocks away from spawn first.

The other missions need gear the bot has to earn first. mine {"count": 8} breaks the ore it scans and needs a pickaxe of the ore's tier. drill needs a pickaxe and a prospected vein, which needs a charged HV prospector (mid-game): on a fresh install it pauses with DRILL_NEEDS_PROSPECT (see MISSIONS.md § drill).

The bot also yields on its own: low health → home, worn tool → hot-swap, and any manual movement input → PAUSED, so you can take over just by moving.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
• Multiple bots / co-op fleet: FLEET_PLAYBOOK.md + BOT_INSTANCE_SETUP.md.
  • Writing missions/capabilities/ext plugins: EXTENDING.md.
  • The three test layers incl. in-game arenas: TESTING.md.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The bridge binds loopback only (127.0.0.1:<port>); override via the mc_bridge_host GlobalVar only if you know what you're exposing.
  • The bot's world knowledge (waypoints, storages, prospected veins) persists to <Macros>/mc_world.json; the NDJSON journal is <Macros>/miner.ndjson (get_logs tails it).
  • Headless screenshots need enableVsync:false in the instance's options.txt (otherwise off-screen frames go stale). Screenshots and GUI clicks: Eyes & hands.

docs.title: Testing — the three layers
docs.text:
The bot is tested at three levels. There is no CI. The versioned git hooks (just hooks) are the gate, and they run layer 1. Layers 2 and 3 need a live game, so you run them by hand before merging in-game behaviour changes.

Layer What Runs where Command 1. Mock suite Pure domain logic, capability and mission loops on the mock runtime; the Python host-tool suites; the mutants of the host-tool guards git hooks: pre-commit the TS half and the gate-tag lint, pre-push all of it just check-ts, just check 2. Facade smoke The raw-Java facade methods, executed in the real worker a live bot ./gerda smoke 3. Arena gate Real missions in built arenas, plus navigator leg benches a live, opped test bot just gate-live (./gerda gate)

pre-commit runs just check-ts, the TS half of just check plus the gate-tag lint (just gate-tags), so a commit takes seconds; pre-push runs the full just check (the TS half again, the Python suites and the mutants, just mutants), builds the bundle and validates it (just validate-bundle: the deploy step's checks, validate_bundle() in scripts/ops/sync.py). Pre-push builds from the checkout, so it refuses to push a commit other than HEAD that shares history with it — check out the commit you push. (A maintainer-only leak scan also runs when scripts/private/ exists; a fork skips it.) Run from a shell without the dev shell's tools (an IDE, a plain terminal), a hook re-enters the flake dev shell through nix develop when nix is installed; without nix it runs as is. Do not skip either hook with --no-verify. Pre-push writes its output to pre-push.log in the worktree's git dir (git rev-parse --git-path pre-push.log) and prints one summary line. On failure it prints the failing command and the last 40 log lines. just smoke-clean (./gerda smoke-clean) is a separate check: it brings the toolchain up on a clean distro in a rootless container.

docs.title: Layer 1 — the mock suite
docs.text:
just check = just check-ts (the gate-tag lint, then bun run check: tsc --noEmit + biome check + the defensive-code checker + vitest) plus the Python unittest suites (just test-py) plus the mutants of the host-tool guards (just mutants, below).

Test count. This is the one place the docs state it: over 1,000 vitest tests in test-ts/ and about 870 Python tests (scripts/tests/ for host tooling, scripts/objective/tests/ for the objective engine). Count them yourself with node_modules/.bin/vitest list and just test-py.

The vitest suites run the pure shared/domain/ logic and every capability and mission against core/runtime/mock.ts, which implements the same interface as the real runtime, so it cannot drift. The planner also has property-based tests (fast-check) for legality, determinism and completeness on generated terrain. The suite boots no game.

It does not cover live movement physics, synthetic-input reach, mod-API calls or the service harness. Layers 2 and 3 do.

docs.title: Mutants of the host-tool guards
docs.text:
A guard in a host tool — a check in the sandbox scripts (scripts/sandbox/sbx.sh, provision.sh, Containerfile), the arena check rules in scripts/dev/arena.py, the --min-luma gate of scripts/rig/motion_probe.py — counts as tested only when some test goes red without it. We keep that evidence as data. A mutant is one literal edit that breaks one guarded line, together with the tests that must then fail and the message they must print. scripts/dev/mutants.py runs them.

  • Tags. Every die-shaped line in those files carries # gate:<id> or # not-a-gate: <reason> (a reason of three or more words). Die-shaped is a fixed list of failure shapes the lint knows: in shell every return/exit but 0, every || but || true, every false, fail helper, unguarded test/[, and checksum check; in a Containerfile every RUN; in the listed Python functions every return, raise, assert, exit call and .append. A guard in another shape is not flagged — for example a bare grep -q, cmp or diff under set -e, (( … )), ${1:?}, a trap … ERR, or a Python failure recorded with += or ok = False. Such a guard counts as tested only when its author tags it and a reviewer checks that, so the lint is a floor, not a proof that every guard is known. Every gate tagged today has a mutant that kills it. A file in the scope where the rule finds nothing fails the lint. A tag on a comment-only line covers the next line and its \ continuations.
  • Mutant files are scripts/dev/mutants/<area>.toml: the gate ids ([gates]), the files the lint reads ([scope]), and one mutant table per edit — file, anchor (the text to replace; it must occur exactly once), replace, test (test ids), expect_message (substrings the failing run prints) and expect_failures (the exact number of failing tests).
  • just gate-tags (pre-commit) fails on an untagged die-shaped line, a gate:<id> that no mutant file declares, a declared gate id that no line carries, and a mutant whose anchor does not occur exactly once, is not on a line tagged with its gate id, or names a test that does not exist.
  • just mutants [area [mutant ...]] (pre-push) copies the tree to a temp dir per mutant — the checkout is never changed — makes the edit and runs the named tests. Each area first prints a CONTROL row: the same tests on an unedited copy, with their exit code and Ran N tests line. A red CONTROL stops the run, because a red run of a mutant only means something when the same tests pass without the edit. Then one row per mutant: killed (the only green result), survived, wrong_failure, or a broken mutant (anchor_missing, anchor_ambiguous, unparsable, run_failed, skipped). python3 scripts/dev/mutants.py list prints every mutant.

Adding a guard: tag the line # gate:<id>, write the test that fails without it, and add the mutant that removes exactly that guard; just gate-tags and just mutants <area> <name> show that it works.

docs.title: Layer 2 — facade smoke (./gerda smoke)
docs.text:
Some facade methods call raw Java (player sensors via SRG names, eat/respawn on the render thread). They can pass the mock suite and still fail in-game on a wrong SRG name or a wrong-thread closure. scripts/ops/facade_smoke.py runs the worker's smoke command (src/bot/capabilities/diagnostics.ts), which executes those probes in the real worker and reports one line per check. It exits non-zero on any failure. Run it when you touch src/core/runtime/. --eat also takes one real bite and verifies that food rose. Needs a running bot; --port picks one other than the loopback default 55544:

./gerda smoke --port 55545          # read-only probes, one line per check
./gerda smoke --port 55545 --json   # the same, machine-readable

docs.title: Layer 3 — the arena gate (just gate-live)
docs.text:
scripts/dev/gate_live.py builds and runs the declarative test arenas (scenarios/arenas/*.json) against a connected bot and rolls every PASS/FAIL into one exit code.

just gate-live                       # FULL gate: every asserting arena + navigator leg benches
just gate-live --quick               # the curated 5-arena core, no benches
just gate-live mine-vein drill-vein  # a named subset (no benches)
just gate-live --bench-only          # only the navigator leg benches
python scripts/dev/gate_live.py --port <port> …  # target a specific bot (default 55544; ports: mc-bots.json)
python scripts/dev/gate_live.py --list           # list arenas/benches + gate status

The full gate set is derived: every arena whose spec asserts (non-empty expect.events, or checks) is gated. Build-only fixtures (bridge-engine, parkour-gap2, mine-down, …) are left out, because they would pass trivially. The navigator's movement sub-machines are gated by the leg benches (scenarios/bench/*.json with legs): each leg is driven through the nav probe, and PASS = arrived (one retry allowed, because live physics is noisy). Mission benches (drill-throughput, ore-room) measure throughput and stay out of the gate.

Each arena (spec: scripts/dev/arena.py) builds a structure, kits and teleports the bot, starts a mission, and asserts that the expected log events fire with no TRANSITION → ERROR within a timeout. A missing event or an ERROR is a FAIL. gate_live.py clears each arena's region afterwards, pass or fail.

Build and clean each hold a /forceload ticket on the arena's chunks while they write, so an arena far from every player (a fresh world, where nobody has been near 0,0) is loaded before the first /fill. The ticket is removed when the writes are done.

Exit codes: 0 all passed · 1 one or more failed · 2 no verdict: preflight failed (no bot on the bridge), or the bridge stopped answering mid-gate. In the second case the summary lists the arenas that did not run; check the client's latest.log, then run those by name.

Give it CPU. A worker tick that takes seconds (software rendering, a loaded host) makes missions time out, and the arenas FAIL for that reason, not for the mission logic. Run the gate on a machine with a real GPU or an idle CPU.

Use an opped test bot. Arena setup uses operator commands (/fill, /tp, kit items). Fleet bots are non-op players, so op a dedicated test bot for the session and de-op it when done (FLEET_PLAYBOOK). The gate is not meant for headless CI.

Use a clean sandbox. Arenas build at fixed world coordinates. On a live world those coordinates can land inside terrain or your base, and the bot's world memory (known hazards, veins) can change what a mission does. Build a flat test area and run the gate there.

Check it is the bot, not you. The default bridge port (55544) can be your own client. The preflight prints the connected player name — confirm it is the test bot.

docs.title: Adding an arena
docs.text:
Add scenarios/arenas/<name>.json (ops + mission + expect.events); a non-empty expect.events puts it in the full gate. Every key and op, with its default and the code that reads it: SCENARIOS.md. scenarios/scenario.schema.json holds the shape of every scenario file, and scripts/tests/test_scenario_schema.py checks each tracked file against it.

An arena can also assert game state with no mission: checks, a list of jeval expressions with the JSON value each must return. A known_bad arena marks its wrong-on-purpose checks "wrong": true: a marked check passes only on a different value from a jeval that succeeded, and every other check must pass as usual (no verdict is inverted). This is the mod-testing path, with a worked GregTech CEu pair (gtceu-ore-harvest-tier and its known-bad twin): MOD_TESTING.md. Add it to CORE in scripts/dev/gate_live.py only if it guards a core behaviour that breaks easily (keep --quick small). Arenas must not overlap in world space: each build clears only its own region.

A film set is not an arena. Staging captured from the live world lives in scenarios/sets/<name>.json (no mission/plan/expect, plus a snapshot declaration) and is outside the gate. See RIG.md.

Assert behaviours, not state-dependent side effects. expect.events should name events the mission emits on every run: ORE_FOUND, DRILL_VEIN_REACHED, GOTO_ARRIVED, PLACE_CELL. Do not assert events that depend on accumulated world state or config latches. WAYPOINT is deduplicated against existing vein markers within cfg.scan.veinRadius, and VEINS_DEPLETED needs the mining slice's exhausted latch plus nearby waypoints. The mock suite covers those. This is why mine-vein/drill-vein assert only the mined/reached event.

docs.title: Navigator benches
docs.text: scripts/dev/navbench.py (./gerda bench) measures the navigator in-game: leg benches for arrival and wall-clock ticks, planner A/B (A* vs D* Lite), and whole-mission throughput. See navbench.md.

docs.title: Navigator benchmarks
docs.text:
The navigator is the part of Gerda Bot that moves the player: walking, climbing, dropping down, routing around obstacles and jumping gaps. navbench measures it in the live game on small, repeatable courses. A bench answers three questions:

  • Does the bot arrive? Every run counts as arrived or not.
  • How fast? Time is in game ticks (20 ticks = 1 second). The bench drives the bot at the same per-tick cadence as a real mission, so ticks are an honest proxy for wall-clock time.
  • Which planner is faster here? A* is the default planner. D* Lite is optional, and a bench can race the two on the same course.

Run the benches after you change movement code or navigator tuning, to confirm the change did not make the bot slower or less reliable. The leg benches also run in the live arena gate (just gate-live), where PASS = arrived. See TESTING.md.

docs.title: Before you run
docs.text:
The benches use the same setup as the arena gate:

  • A connected, opped test bot. A bench builds its course with operator commands (/fill, /tp, kit items). That is test setup only — missions never use operator commands. Op the test bot for the session and de-op it when you finish.
  • A clean, flat test area. Each course builds at fixed world coordinates. On a lived-in world those coordinates can land in terrain or in your base.
  • The right client. By default the bench drives the client on bridge port 55544, and that can be your own game client. Pass --port <port> to drive a fleet bot instead. The port must be in mc-bots.json, because a mission bench writes its ore marker into that bot's own world store. Either way, confirm that the connected player is the test bot.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
./gerda bench list              # list the benches
./gerda bench run flat          # run one bench
./gerda bench run --all         # run every bench
./gerda bench build flat        # only build the course (to look at it in-game)
./gerda bench run flat --port 55545   # drive the bot on bridge port 55545

./gerda bench is a shortcut for python scripts/dev/navbench.py.

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
Each course runs several times: 3 times for a leg bench, 2 for a mission bench. For each leg (or mission) and planner, the report prints:

  • the median ticks of the runs that arrived;
  • the arrival count, for example 3/3 (for a mission bench: how many runs mined the area out).

When a bench races two planners, the report also prints the ratio of their medians (below 1.0 means the second planner is faster). Live physics is noisy, so compare medians, not single runs, and repeat a run before you trust a small difference.

docs.title: Leg benches
docs.text:
A leg bench drives the bot from a start point to a goal and isolates one kind of movement. Each course sits over a catch floor, so a missed jump is a survivable fall, not a death.

bench leg(s) what it tests flat flat12, flat24 straight sprint over 12 and 24 blocks climb climb6 a 6-step staircase up descend descend6 a 6-step staircase down (1-block drops) detour around routing around a wall that blocks the straight line gap jump3 a sprint-jump over a 2-block void

docs.title: Mission benches
docs.text:
A mission bench runs a whole mission once per planner and measures the ticks from mission start until the area is mined out. It shows how navigation speed adds up in real work: walking to the ore, breaking it, and moving between blocks. Mission benches measure throughput only, so they are not part of the arena gate.

  • drill-throughput — the drill mission walks to an iron cluster buried in a small stone hill, digs a shaft down to it and mines it out, picking up the drops.
  • ore-room — the mine mission clears a 7×5 slab of iron ore, one block high, in open air. The measure is that no ore is left. The item count is lower than 35, because some drops fall into the holes the bot mines.

docs.title: Writing a bench
docs.text:
A bench is one JSON file in scenarios/bench/<name>.json:

{
  "desc": "What the course tests.",
  "ops": [
    { "op": "fill", "from": [39, 88, -1], "to": [70, 88, 3], "block": "minecraft:stone" },
    { "op": "give", "item": "minecraft:diamond_pickaxe" }
  ],
  "start": [41, 89, 1],
  "legs": [ { "name": "flat12", "to": [53, 89, 1] } ],
  "impls": ["astar", "dstar"],
  "repeats": 3,
  "timeout": 30
}
  • ops builds the course and kits the bot. It uses the same operations as the arena specs (clear, fill, clearinv, give, select, …). The runner teleports the bot to start before every run, so the ops do not place the player.
  • legs lists the goals to drive to from start.
  • impls picks the planners: astar (the default) and/or dstar.
  • repeats, timeout and arrival are optional.
  • For a mission bench, replace legs with "mission": { "name": "mine", "params": {} }.

Every key, its default and the code that reads it: SCENARIOS.md § Benches.

Courses must not overlap: each build clears only its own region. Put a new course clear of the existing ones.

docs.title: Gerda vs Baritone
docs.text:
We raced the navigator against Baritone on the same legs, 3 runs per leg. The table shows median ticks; lower is faster.

leg Gerda Baritone flat12 36 37 flat24 78 79 climb6 62 58 descend6 43 42 around 115 102 jump3 29 29
  • Reliability is equal. Both arrive on all six legs.
  • Speed is equal on flat ground, descents and the gap. Gerda is 7% slower on the climb and 13% slower on the detour.

Both gaps are the cost of deliberate safety choices:

  • The bot sprints only with clear ground ahead. Before it sprints, the navigator checks that the next two cells are safe to run on. This stops the bot from sliding off a short bridge, and it keeps the bot on its line through diagonal corners. A looser check saves a few ticks on the detour but makes the bot overshoot the corner and miss the goal.
  • Climbing is limited by jump timing. The bot keeps sprinting through each stair jump and clears one stair per jump, whatever its speed. The remaining gap is the delay between landing and the next jump, about 0.7 ticks per stair.
